docs.title: HIV Informatics
docs.text: Alejandro Rafael Gener A dissertation submitted to the Faculty of the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, Baylor College of Medicine, in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy. Houston, Texas, September 22, 2021.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Advances in the study of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) track with advances in nucleic acid sequencing. However, there remains no unified framework for approaching the types of sequences seen across the HIV replication cycle, preventing comprehensive studies in more complex HIV experimental systems. Overly simplified models of HIV proviral and virion genomes, ignorance of HIV splice isoforms, and inconsistent reagent verification prevent the observation of HIV heterogeneity by way of sequence variability, obscuring biological insights. The establishment of HIV Informatics as a framework for approaching HIV sequence variability across HIV’s diverse forms enables investigators and clinicians to maximize the information gained from their assays. In this dissertation, I:

  • Established HIV Informatics as a framework unifying HIV models, nucleic acid (re)sequencing, bioinformatics, and validation to maximize the HIV information gained from assays

  • Evaluated modern sequencing methods for recovering HIV-1 information from key reagents/models

  • Found in vitro HIV-1 transductions are more like transfections with HIV-1 virions delivering packaged HIV-1 transcripts from 293T producer cells to CD4+ T cells isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells.

  • Defined comprehensive HIV transcript models from long- and short-read data, enabling HIV-1 gene expression studies

  • Identified up to 15 new putative HIV-1 proteins conserved across HIV-1 and simian immunodeficiency viruses 

  • Leveraged insights from above to follow HIV-1 sequence variability during acute HIV-1 encephalopathy in HIV patients

This dissertation is divided into three parts. “Part One: HIV, HIV (re)sequencing, and a new framework to maximize HIV information from samples” serves as an introduction, divided into four chapters. Chapter 1 describes select information about what is known about HIV/AIDS and focuses our discussion on HIV. Chapter 2 describes select methods used to elucidate HIV information (HIV informatics, with a little “i”) in experimental and clinical settings. Chapter 3 introduces HIV Informatics (big “I”) as a framework unifying HIV models, nucleic acid (re)sequencing, bioinformatics, and validation to maximize the HIV information gained from assays. Chapter 4 discusses the problems that will be addressed in the subsequent chapters. I begin the discussion of my experimental findings in “Part Two: Maximizing HIV sequencing information from control samples and model systems”. This part includes Chapter 5, where I discuss advances in HIV DNA space. We then transition into the RNA space, where we discuss advances such as HIV mRNA models (Chapter 6) and HIV virion mRNA (Chapter 7). This part concludes by analyzing HIV RNA with LTR phasing in Chapter 8, with the paradigm-shifting finding that in vitro HIV-1 transductions are more like transfections with HIV-1 virions delivering packaged HIV-1 transcripts from 293T producer cells to CD4+ T cells isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells. “Part Three: Maximizing HIV sequence information from heterogeneous samples” includes a discussion about interrogating HIV in non-model systems in Chapter 9, specifically recovering HIV information from post-mortem HIV encephalopathy patients with single-nuclear RNA sequencing. We were able to follow limited HIV evolution in noisy samples, as well as detect the new isoforms seen in Chapter 6, illustrating the benefit of HIV Informatics to enable the study of HIV across the spectrum of HIV samples just short of clinical samples. This dissertation concludes in Chapter 10 with a discussion and future directions, including a call to action for third-party validation of findings presented herein.

docs.title: Chapter 1: What we know believe about HIV
Abstract
docs.text: Chapter 1 of HIV Informatics introduces select information about the known biology of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1). All discussions of HIV in this dissertation pertain to HIV-1, unless otherwise specified. Also included is a brief discussion of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Details of clinical management and psychosocial determinants of health (Ghosn et al. 2018) for people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) or at risk of acquiring HIV fall outside the scope of this dissertation and are not discussed.

docs.title: AIDS, and the discovery of HIV
docs.text:
The first reported cases of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) came as a short case report describing opportunistic infections that seemed out of place (CDC 1981). Five young male patients all identified as “homosexual” had multiple opportunistic infections usually only seen in immunocompromised patients. Their infections included Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP1) (Walzer et al. 1974), oral mucosal candidiasis, and cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections. These patients were believed to be immunocompromised due to lowered immune cell function, in absence of any obvious primary cause (e.g., a hematological cancer which might have directly affected immune cells). These 5 young men would unfortunately not be the last. AIDS soon appeared in heterosexual populations including but not limited to Haitian immigrants in New York, hemophiliacs, patients receiving blood-derived products, babies from mothers who would occasionally develop AIDS too. Patterns of spread were beginning to emerge with each new case report.

The Editorial Note at the end of the first case report hypothesized that these men had an acquired cause of immune disfunction (CDC 1981). But with AIDS patients susceptible to so many pathogens, which one was the causative agent? It is helpful to understand how microbiologists went about proving an infectious agent was pathogenic. This was done by observing Koch’s Postulates. Koch’s Postulates, developed by Robert Koch, set the gold standard for establishing a microbiological etiology for infection and disease, summarized in a seminar prepared by Stanley Falkow in 1988 (Falkow 2004)). These included: 1.) the agent occurs in every individual with disease, and 2.) is not seen in healthy individuals, and 3.) the agent, when cultured, can recapitulate infection and disease in healthy individuals exposed to the agent. Originally based on Koch’s work with tuberculosis and anthrax, these postulates were later expanded to encompass non-bacterial pathogens, including viruses. For initial studies of suspected deadly pathogens, in vitro cell-culture infection models and in vivo disease models non-human infection models were acceptable surrogates to human studies which were not possible because of ethical reasons (e.g., the Nuremberg Code). During the early days of the AIDS epidemic, clinical samples from AIDS and pre-AIDS patients were the first sources of early material harboring potential AIDS-causing agent(s).

The race was on to find the causative agent(s) of AIDS. Two important papers came out in the same issue of the journal Science on May 20, 1983. One from the Americans led by Robert Gallo at the National Cancer Center, and another from a group of French researchers at the Pasteur Institute. The Americans who had recently discovered Human T-Cell Leukemia Virus (HTLV-1) identified HTLV-1 in an AIDS patient (Gallo et al. 1983). This led them to believe that an HTLV-like virus might be the cause of AIDS. The French group provided strong evidence at the time that the virus they had found, which they called lymphadenopathy-associated virus (LAV), was not HTLV (Barré-Sinoussi et al. 1983). Then in 1984 four Science papers by Gallo and collaborators identified an HTLV-like virus in AIDS patients, and in patients at risk of AIDS who would later contract AIDS (termed pre-AIDS patients) (Popovic et al. 1984) (Sarngadharan et al. 1984) (Schüpbach et al. 1984) (Gallo et al. 1984). They believed this was a new virus, HTLV-III. However it was in fact HIV-1. The Americans were not the first to isolate HIV-1 (Cohen and Enserink 2008), but they did provide strong evidence that HIV-1 was the causative agent of AIDS (Marx 1984).

The World Health Organization maintains statistics for HIV globally (https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/hiv-aids). To date, 76 million people have contracted HIV, and 33 million people have died from HIV/AIDS. At the end of 2019, there were 38 million people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA). This represents the global prevalence of HIV. Africa remains most severely affected, accounting for more than two-thirds of HIV cases globally, with 1 in every 25 adults (3.7%) living with HIV. The number of new HIV cases in 2019 was 1.7 million. In the US, HIV stats are maintained by the Department of Health & Human Services and supported by the Minority HIV/AIDS Fund on HIV.gov (https://www.hiv.gov/hiv-basics/overview/data-and-trends/statistics). About 1.2 million people were living with HIV in the US, and there were an estimated 36,400 new HIV infections in 2018.

The United Nations currently has a “90-90-90” strategy with the following goals to end the AIDS epidemic. By 2020, 1.) at least 90% of PLWHA will know their HIV status, 2.) at least 90% of PLWHA will receive sustained combined antiretroviral therapy (cART), and 3.) 90% of PLWHA on cART will achieve viral suppression (UNAIDS). An important paradigm shift to facilitate 90-90-90 is test and treat, where people at risk of acquiring HIV are diagnosed if positive and are then linked to care (Ghosn et al. 2018). PLWHA are living longer thanks to earlier diagnosing and better medications (Lohse and Obel 2016; Samji et al. 2013). This has paradoxically led to PLWH having increased risk of having non-AIDS comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease and cancer (Ghosn et al. 2018), and renal disease (Wyatt and Klotman 2016), among others.

docs.title: HIV replication cycle
docs.text: This section summarizes the HIV replication cycle, and wrote it considering several review sources, including ViralZone (Swiss South Africa Joint Research Programme. n.d.) (https://viralzone.expasy.org/5096), the HIV InSite Knowledgebase (University of California, San Francisco) (http://hivinsite.ucsf.edu/InSite?page=KB), and the book HIV and the Pathogenesis of AIDS by Jay A. Levy (Levy 2007).

docs.title: HIV virion
docs.text:
We begin arbitrarily with the HIV virion. Mature HIV-1 virion particles are membrane-bound, with embedded viral glycoprotein gp120, and a non-covalently associated embedded viral protein gp41 (together called the HIV glycoprotein complex). Host proteins such as ICAM-1 are known to co-occur and are believed to contribute to cell tropism by interacting with target cell integrins. The HIV membrane is sensitive to detergent, desiccation, and changes in temperature, salt, and pH deviating from host physiology, rendering individual virions fragile compared to non-enveloped viruses. These weaknesses have been explored with microbicide development but have so far not been effective at reducing HIV transmission.

Interior to the virion membrane, mature particles are believed to contain HIV protease-cleaved HIV gene products, two full-length unspliced HIV-1 mRNA viral genome equivalents, and rarely host RNAs. Well-characterized major cleavage products (mature peptides, or GenBank record tag “mat_peptide”) from Gag polyprotein include the structural proteins: capsid protein (p17; CA), matrix protein (p24; MA), and nucleocapsid (NC; p7). Minor cleavage products include p1, p2, p6. Cleavage products from the Gag-Pol polyprotein include those (except p6) with Gag-Pol transframe peptide, protease (PR; aspartic peptidase), p51 subunit of reverse transcriptase, and p66 subunit of reverse transcriptase with p15 RNAse H domain, and p31 integrase. A ribosomal frame shift occurs near the end of p1 and the beginning of p6 which causes a shift from gag2 to pol reading frame, enabling the pol segment of Gag-Pol to be expressed instead of Gag. The Pol polyprotein is not believed to occur independently of Gag (which excludes Pol) or Gag-Pol. The HIV accessory proteins Vif, Vpr, Vpu, Rev, and Nef are also found in HIV virions. Accessory viral proteins are not essential for viral replication. They are reviewed in greater detail below.

Each mature virion is commonly modeled as having two copies of full-length unspliced HIV-1 (+)-sense coding mRNA. This is believed to be a direct transcript from full-length replication-competent HIV-1 provirus. There is some evidence that diploidy need not be essential, or at least need not be tied to reverse transcription (Jones, Allan, and Temin 1994; Panganiban and Fiore 1988; van Wamel and Berkhout 1998). Another interpretation of the above is that virion diploidy is not essential, which leaves room for aneuploidy via stochastic packaging of viral mRNAs. The HIV genome, reference genomes, and gene models are discussed later in this dissertation.

docs.title: HIV tropism (pre-entry)
docs.text:
The mechanism of viral tropism, or how virions select cells to first attach to and then infect after entry, is well-studied. It is divided into roughly two kinds of tropism: receptor-mediated and receptor-independent. Receptor-mediated tropism includes interactions between HIV glycoprotein complexes, mediated by gp120, first binding to attachment receptors such as CD4 (Maddon et al. 1986), a major host-expressed HIV receptor. Host ICAM-1 on the HIV virion membrane may also interact with target cell integrins such as LFA1 (https://viralzone.expasy.org/247). Cells expressing CD4 include T-lymphocytes (“T cells”), macrophages, dendritic cells (https://viralzone.expasy.org/247). Other adhesion receptors and some of the cells which express them include: DC-SIGN expressed by dendritic cells (da Silva, Segat, and Crovella 2011); CLEC4M (also known as L-SIGN) expressed by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells and cells in the lymph node (probably dendritic cells) (da Silva et al. 2011); heparan sulfate expressed by many cell types (Crublet et al. 2008).

Subsequent entry via membrane fusion is mediated by interaction between gp41 and with host cell-expressed co-receptors such as CCR5 (R5) and CXCR4 (X4). One hypothesized mechanism for entry is clathrin-mediated endocytosis (https://viralzone.expasy.org/957?outline=all_by_species), although there is some evidence that this is not the only mechanism HIV-1 may use for entry (Permanyer, Ballana, and Esté 2010). After attachment of gp120 to CD4 or ICAM-1 to integrins, gp41 mediates fusion between virion and target cell membranes. The fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide (also called T-20) works by interfering with gp41 conformational changes necessary for membrane fusion (Arts et al. 2012) (Zhang et al. 2018). An important point to consider which limits the applicability of fusion inhibitors clinically is that HIV tropism often shifts during infection. This shift may have important prognostic consequence; X4-tropic trains are often seen later in the natural course of HV infection, and are considered worse (Verhofstede, Nijhuis, and Vandekerckhove 2012). Receptor-independent infection occurs by cytopathic effects such as HIV-mediated syncytia formed between cells infected with CXCR4-tropic HIV and neighboring cells.

Several CD4- cell types have also been found to be susceptible to HIV infection in vitro (Table 3.8 (Levy 2007)). These included: fetal astrocytes, brain-derived capillary endothelial cells, brain microglia (which will be revisited in Chapter 8), NK cells, primary skin fibroblasts fetal adrenal cells, follicular dendritic cells, hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, trophoblast cells, cervical epithelial cell lines. Cancer cell lines such as the following have also been shown to be susceptible to infection independently of CD4 expression: the SK-N-Mc neuroblastoma cell line, the HOS osteosarcoma cell line, the RD rhabdomyosarcoma cell line, hepatocellular carcinoma cells, bowel adenocarcinoma cells. In vivo studies suggested that bowel epithelium, renal epithelium, dental pulp fibroblasts, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes (which will be revisit in Chapter 8) were all susceptible to HIV. The number of tissues purported to support various stages of HIV replication is ever growing. These reservoirs can be sources of low-level viral replication and re-seeding after discontinuation of antiviral therapy, and represent an important challenge to achieving a sterilizing cure (Fletcher et al. 2014) (Lorenzo-Redondo et al. 2016) (Ghosn et al. 2018). A sterilizing cure would mean elimination of HIV from the body and no need to continued antiviral therapy, as opposed to a functional cure which we have currently when HIV medications are given to patients earlier to prevent HIV replication and subsequent immune dysregulation. Despite promising gene therapy results to change expression of HIV co-receptors by introducing Δ32 mutations into the CCR5 co-receptors of allogenic hematopeotic stem cells in the context of separately indicated bone marrow transplants, there currently remains no sterilizing cure for HIV infection.

docs.title: Post-entry
docs.text: Within 40 minutes of fusion (Swiss South Africa Joint Research Programme. n.d.), encapsidated viral mRNA is transported to the nucleus via dynein along microtubules (Gaudin et al. 2013; McDonald et al. 2002). Premature capsid destabilization (e.g., Cyp A inhibition, CPSF6 (Lee et al. 2010), Mx2 (Goujon et al. 2013), and TRIM5α expression in some non-human primates (Nakayama and Shioda 2010)) may lead to abortive infection. This exposes viral mRNA prematurely in the infected cell, stimulating host cell antiviral response. Appropriately timed uncoating delivers the RT complex (discussed below) to the nucleus for import, protecting nascent HIV cDNA from host antiviral sensors (Ambrose and Aiken 2014).

docs.title: Reverse transcription
docs.text:
The process of HIV-1 reverse transcription (RT) is well-studied, reviewed in (Hu and Hughes 2012) and at ViralZone (SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics n.d.) (Add mobile elements III). Briefly, HIV-1 RT’s RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity is primed by a lysine tRNA binding to the primer-binding site (PBS) in the forward/coding/(+)-sense mRNA in the reverse/reverse-complimentary/(-)-sense orientation (Chapter 1 Figure 2: HIV-1 reverse transcription and LTR homogenization). RT synthesizes the reverse-complimentary cDNA from the PBS to the end of the 5’ R repeat and reaches a minus strand strong stop. RNAse H activity from the p66 subunit of RT degrades the complimentary RNA in the RNA-DNA heteroduplex. The first strand transfer occurs when the synthesized cDNA finds complimentary R sequence at the 3’ end. The template, assumed to be the full-length unspliced genome, is copied by RT. RT RNAse H activity degrades most of the remaining HIV mRNA, except for essential sequences called poly-purine tracks (PPTs). These regions exhibit marginal resistance to initial RNAse H activity. Second strand synthesis by RT is primed by the remaining PPT(s). Once the positive strand strong stop occurs, the PPT(s) give way to RT RNAse H activity. The Lys-tRNA primer is also degraded. A second strand transfer occurs, this time leveraging the PBS (instead of the R). Both cDNA strands are then finished by RT’s DNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity.

Chapter 1 Figure 2: HIV-1 reverse transcription and LTR homogenization.

Homogenization is not exactly copying. It is a (3’ U3)-(5’ R)-(5’ U5) duplication. Consider replacing “copying” with “(3’ U3)-(5’ R)-(5’ U5) duplication”. Adapted from (SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics n.d.).

RT happens on microfilaments in the in the RT complex (RTC) (Greene and Peterlin 2006) and is believed to occur within 8-12 hours post-infection of a host cell (Iordanskiy et al. 2006). HIV cDNA is detectable within 4 hours post infection (hpi) (Hu and Hughes 2012). RT inhibitors exist in two broad classes nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) and non-nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI) (Arts et al. 2012). NRTIs are incorporated by RT into the nascent cDNA strands, leading to chain termination. NNRTIs also inhibit RT, however they do so by allosterically binding outside of RT active site, ultimately inhibiting RT activity. RT is the most error-prone step in HIV replication. Once the first strand of cDNA is made, it is vulnerable to cytidine deamination by host APOBECs (Salter, Bennett, and Smith 2016), which are often packaged in the virion (SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics n.d.). The HIV accessory protein Vif, also known as viral infectivity factor or p23, inhibits APOBECs’ antiviral activity (Swiss South Africa Joint Research Programme. n.d.) (Barraud et al. 2008). RT completion is marked by double-stranded cDNA with identical LTRs. The template HIV genomic mRNA is presumably degraded. Distinguishing between primary HIV mRNAs (from either HIV molecular clones used to transfect virus-producing cells like human embryonic kidney 293T cells OR from reactivated HIV-infected cell lines), reverse-transcribed HIV cDNAs and/or secondary HIV mRNA from “infected” cells was a challenge prior to this dissertation. It was unknown how much primary HIV mRNAs contributed to HIV gene expression signatures in newly infected cells.

docs.title: Integration and entry into latency
docs.text:
Once RT is completed, the pre-integration complex (PIC) containing double-stranded cDNA is transported into the nucleus. Once inside the nucleus, but before integration, the HIV accessory protein Vpr (viral protein R, p15) inhibits antiviral responses like SMC5/6 complex compaction of viral cDNA designed to silence expression from foreign DNA (Dupont et al. 2021). Methylation of HIV cDNA represses further HIV transcription until the methylation is reversed (reviewed (Ruelas and Greene 2013)).

During integration, the HIV cDNA ends are terminally processed by HIV integrase (Hu pharma review) (Arts et al. 2012) (Lesbats, Engelman, and Cherepanov 2016). Following end processing, strand transfer is the limiting factor of HIV integration and establishment of the HIV provirus. Subsequently, HIV proviral mRNA expression may occur, or expression may be silenced as is the case when HIV enters viral latency. Integration inhibitors (Arts et al. 2012) are a newer class of anti-HIV drugs that have become important first line agents used in current combination treatments. Raltegravir was the first FDA-approved integrase inhibitor. These drugs work by inhibiting strand transfer. HIV integration into the host genome, viral latency, and subsequent immune evasion remain the most challenging roadblocks of HIV biology preventing attainment of sterilizing cure (Ghosn et al. 2018). Integrase inhibitors will be discussed in more detail in the “HIV pharmacotherapy” section below.

Discuss unintegrated.. (Meyerhans et al. 2003)

docs.title: Viral reactivation is exit from latency
docs.text: The natural triggers for HIV reactivation, or exit from latency, remain poorly understood. This is in part due to technical limitations studying infected cells once transcription is turned on. For example, virus-producing cell lifespan is shortened to about 2 days (Wei et al. 1995). In vitro studies have found reactivation agents can stimulate HIV mRNA expression (Shirakawa et al. 2013). Pharmacological latency reversal has been explored as a treatment targeting the HIV reservoirs (Ghosn et al. 2018). Agents evaluated included vorinostat (Archin et al. 2012) (Elliott et al. 2014), panobinostat, disulfiram, or romidepsin (Søgaard et al. 2015), or with interleukin 7 (IL-7). Unfortunately, these failed to decrease HIV reservoirs (Ghosn et al. 2018). When paired with a functional immune system, latency reversal is an important part of the “shock and kill” strategy to purge the body’s HIV reservoirs (Katlama et al. 2013) (Deeks et al. 2016) (Bullen et al. 2014) (Ghosn et al. 2018).

docs.title: HIV mRNA expression
docs.text:
HIV mRNA expression begins with transcriptional initiation, which is often abortive. This has been studied extensively from the HIV proviral promoter, located in the U3 portion of the 5’ long terminal repeat (LTR). Host RNA polymerase II is recruited to the 5’ LTR. This process is facilitated when the 5’ LTR DNA is unmethylated. HIV-1 encodes a transactivating factor, Tat, which binds to the TAR element. The TAR element is an RNA hairpin located within the 5’ R repeat. TAR is part of the transcription start site and is present in all complete HIV mRNAs (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020; Ocwieja et al. 2012; Purcell and Martin 1993). The predominant form of Tat protein is believed to be the result of doubly spliced HIV, where two large introns are excised: 1.) the first large intron which would otherwise code for Gag and Gag-Pol, and 2.) the second large intron which would otherwise code for Vpu and Env. An important first functional switch is believed to occur when enough spliced HIV mRNA is made to produce enough Tat. Tat greatly enhances HIV transcription.

Transcriptional initiation is followed by transcriptional elongation, which enables the transcription of full-length unspliced (FLUS) HIV mRNA. Processing of proviral mRNAs is believed to follow the conventions of other host genes. Five prime (5’) capping occurs, followed by intermittent splicing of introns of varying sizes. Splicing is believed to be co-transcriptional. If an intron is skipped, it is retained. Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins are believed to be the products of unspliced HIV mRNA. When an intron containing gag-pol is spliced out, HIV accessory proteins are favored, occasionally with Vpu and Env polyproteins. This stage is commonly called singly spliced HIV. HIV proteins Tat and Rev are produced when an intron containing vpu and env are spliced out (commonly referred to as “multiply spliced”). Some reports suggested that Tat and Rev are made from different mRNAs. Another product of multiply spliced HIV is Nef. Spliced HIV-1 mRNAs are believed to be the preferred isoforms, however, and importantly, the exact rules governing HIV splicing remained undefined prior to this dissertation.

The functions of some of HIV-1’s proteins are known. The product of env, Env/gp160, is a polyprotein which will eventually become the HIV virion envelop glycoprotein, composed of proteolytic cleavage products gp120 and gp41. During Env/gp160 translation, a signal peptide locates Env/gp160 to the lumen of the Golgi, while maintaining Env/gp160’s membrane interaction. Env/gp160 is eventually processed into gp120 and gp41 by host proteases. Gp120 and gp41 eventually make their way onto the surface of infected cells expressing HIV mRNA.

Parallel processes disrupt the host cell plasma membrane protein complex milieux. For example, Vpu and Nef are known to inhibit the cycling of host CD4 (Tokarev and Guatelli 2011), possibly contributing to decreased CD4 function. Nef was shown to downregulate major histocompatibility class I (MHC-I) expression in the HIV-infected cells (Dirk et al. 2016). This contributes to immune system evasion, which is a barrier to proviral elimination.

Another HIV accessory protein viral protein R (Vpr) inhibits the cell cycle, causing it to stop at G2/M. This is believed to facilitate proviral gene expression by ensuring the presence of host factors normally present later in the cell cycle. Vpr has also been posited to help HIV redress some of the DNA damage induced by host APOBECs. This latter activity is believe to be due to Vpr’s preferential binding to host uracil DNA glycosylase 2 (UNG2) and more recently single-strand-selective monofunctional uracil-DNA glycosylase 1 (SMUG1), which leads to preferential incorporation of these host enzymes in HIV virions (Schröfelbauer et al. 2005). As mentioned previously, Vpr has also been show to prevent HIV cDNA silencing (Dupont et al. 2021).

Chapter 1 Figure 5: HIV-1 NL4-3 Rev Response Element). Rev binding to the RRE facilitates the nuclear export of HIV mRNAs containing the env intron/vpu-env segment. This is believed to be an important step to increase the availability of full-length unspliced (FLUS) HIV mRNAs for packaging into virions forming at the host cell plasma membrane (Chapter 1 Figure 6: HIV-1 mRNA expression, Rev switch, virion production).During viral reactivation, a second functional switch occurs when the concentration of HIV Rev protein increases past a certain threshold. Rev is an essential HIV protein that binds to a conserved 2º structure located between the gp120 and gp41 segments of the env intron (my new annotation: vpu-env segment). This Rev Response Element (RRE) is an essential structural feature of the HIV RNA genome (

Chapter 1 Figure 5: HIV-1 NL4-3 Rev Response Element (RRE).

Chapter 1 Figure 6: HIV-1 mRNA expression, Rev switch, virion production.

Once there is enough FLUS HIV mRNA, Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins coordinate recruitment of FLUS HIV mRNA to the site of virion assembly at the host plasma membrane. Accessory factors from the host which may be concurrently packaged into nascent HIV virion include host Lys-tRNA, Lysil-tRNA synthetase (LysRS), and Cyclophilin A (CypA). Cyclophilin A (CypA) is believed to stabilize the HIV virion capsid.

docs.title: HIV polyproteins in host cells and immature virions
docs.text:
The products of HIV mRNA expression are HIV structural polyproteins Gag (GenBank locus_tag: “HIV1gp2”) and Gag-Pol (locus_tag: “HIV1gp1”), as well as accessory proteins Vif (locus_tag: “HIV1gp3”), Vpr (locus_tag: “HIV1gp4”), Tat (locus_tag: “HIV1gp5”), Rev (locus_tag: “HIV1gp6”), Vpu (locus_tag: “HIV1gp7”), envelope precursor Env/gp160 (locus_tag: “HIV1gp8”), and lastly Nef (locus_tag: “HIV1gp9”). These are occasionally cleaved by several host proteases (for example, gp160 is cleaved into gp120 and gp41 by furin). However, the HIV structural polyproteins are believed to remain intact at least until they are packaged into nascent virion. Antisense protein (ASP) from the asp gene (locus_tag: “HIV1gp10”) is a 10th HIV-1 protein-coding gene has been proposed in the antisense orientation overlapping Env.

Gag polyprotein protein concentration is about 10-20x higher than Gag-Pol. Gag-Pol is the product of a ribosomal frame shift occurring near a T homopolymer at the end of the region encoding p7 nucleocapsid (Source: LANL HIV Sequence Database). The result of this frameshift is that there is a one-out-of-ten or one-out-of-twenty chance that the ribosome slips, resulting in a Gag polyprotein shifted into the Pol reading frame to produce Gag-Pol. Importantly, the Gag-Pol open reading frame concludes as it crosses into overlapping Vif sequence. Gag-Pol and Vif are in distinct reading frames. Prior to this dissertation, additional splicing of the Gag-Pol was unknown. Protease inhibitors are an important class of antiretrovirals that helped to break HIV’s unchecked rampage in the late ‘90s (Arts et al. 2012). They were quickly paired with NRTI/NNRTIs in early antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens and remain mainstays in HIV treatment regimens globally. These work by preventing virion maturation.

docs.title: Virion assembly
docs.text: As Rev expression increases, it shifts the balance from more spliced HIV mRNAs like Tat/Rev/Nef-encoding mRNAs to less spliced products like Vif/Vpr-, Vpu/Env-, and Gag-Pol-encoding mRNAs reaching the cytoplasm (Felber, Drysdale, and Pavlakis 1990). These longer mRNAs are believed to be preferentially packaged into virion production zones at the infected cell’s plasma membrane. These interactions are mediated by the NC domain of Gag (D’Souza and Summers 2005; El Meshri et al. 2015). RNA hairpins in the 5’ end of the virus are believed to mediate HIV dimer “kissing,” or pairing of two HIV genome copies for incorporation into virion (Paillart et al. 1996). The process of Gag shell assembly takes about 10 minutes (Jouvenet, Bieniasz, and Simon 2008). Budding, or pinching off, of Gag-HIV gRNA complexes which will form immature virion, occurs within about 15 minutes later (Ivanchenko et al. 2009).

docs.title: Virion maturation
docs.text: Budding virion progresses through a maturation process that is incompletely understood. However, it is believed that HIV protease spontaneously activates, and subsequently cleaves the HIV polyproteins into their final forms. This brings about p17, p24, p1, p2, p7, p6 from Gag, as well as p17, p24, p1, p2, p7, the Gag-Pol transframe peptide, PR, p55 and p61 RT, and p31 IN from Gag-Pol.

docs.title: The HIV-1 genome
docs.text:
Chapter 1 Figure 4: HIV-1 viral genome). DNA basing (ACGT) is often preferred to RNA basing (ACGU); a holdover from older bioinformatics tools. Spliced HIV mRNAs are considered sub-genomic, and were not included in genome reference materials prior to this dissertation.All the previously mentioned HIV parts are encoded by the HIV genome. The HIV-1 genome used to be more commonly modeled as a 9.7 kb proviral sequence (Chapter 1 Figure 3: HIV-1 proviral genome), but now is most often modeled as an approximately 9.2 kilobase-long (kb) full-length unspliced (FLUS) mRNA entity (

Chapter 1 Figure 4: HIV-1 viral genome.

Figure made in SnapGene.

Chapter 1 Figure 3: HIV-1 proviral genome.

Figure made in SnapGene.

The two main HIV-1 reference genomes are K03455 and NC_001802. Both are based on HXB2, cloned from one of the earliest clinical isolates of HIV-1 (reviewed in (Gener et al. 2021). The Los Alamos National Laboratory’s HIV Sequence Database uses K03455 (Abfalterer et al. 2018). K03455 is represented in GenBank as K03455.1. This reference is organized as a proviral sequence, with full-length 5’ and 3’ LTRs.

Chapter 1 Figure 1: New HIV-1 Genomes by Sampling Year) and are also made available through the HIV Sequence Database The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) and National Library of Medicine (NLM) at the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) maintains a slightly different HIV-1 reference, the RefSeq entry for HIV NC_001802.1. NC_001802.1 differs from K03455.1 in two ways. K03455.1 is a proviral reference model and includes full-length LTRs. NC_001802.1 is modeled after HIV mRNA, and as such maintains an R-U5-HIV-U3-R structure. NC_001802.1 also has a point mutation in the HIV gene body (between the divided LTRs) (Gener and Kimata 2019). Breaking up the LTRs as 5’ leader and 3’ terminal segments is beneficial for short-read HIV sequencing. In addition to the main references, additional group and subgroup references are available. Full-length HIV-1 genomes are continually deposited into GeneBank ((Abfalterer et al. 2018). Obtaining HIV information from HIV sequencing is a major topic and will be discussed later in this dissertation.

docs.title: Information conservation across the HIV genome
docs.text: Others have noted differences in relative information conservation across the HIV genome. Different parts are believed to be under different selective pressures. For example, essential enzyme activities are known to make up the most conserved loci in the HIV genome. As such, these are under strong negative selection. Conversely, hypervariable regions occur at variable loops, V1-V5 in gp160/gp120. These areas are under pressure to change to evade the hosts humoral immune system (strong positive selection).

docs.title: HIV-1 pharmacotherapy
docs.text:
The previous text in this chapter described select antiretroviral therapy (ART) agents and their mechanisms of action in isolation. However, it is important to understand the historical progress made developing each drug, as well as how each has been used in combination with other HIV medications (Arts et al. 2012).

There have been four major revolutions in HIV/AIDS therapy since the causative agent of AIDS was given a name (Ghosn et al. 2018). The advent of protease inhibitors (PIs) in 1996 heralded the first revolution in HIV/AIDS care. PIs were tried in combination with one and then two nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase (NRTI) inhibitors. This combination therapy was called highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and improved the prognosis of PLWHA which had previously otherwise been grim (Palella et al. 1998).

Riding the wave of effective viral suppression, observational studies (Donnell et al. 2010; Montaner et al. 2010; Quinn et al. 2000; Rodger et al. 2016) culminating in the HPTN 052 study (Cohen et al. 2011, 2016; Cohen, Gamble, and McCauley 2020) supported the extensibility of a new cART (multiple ART medicines with improved toxicity profiles physically combined into fewer pills) to both keep HIV+ people healthier longer, while decreasing their chance of transmission if viral suppression was achieved (Bavinton et al. 2018; Cohen et al. 2016; Rodger et al. 2019). In the HPTN 052 study, HIV serodiscordant couples (couples in which one partner had HIV, while the other did not) had a 96% reduction in the risk of HIV transmission (Cohen et al. 2016; Rodger et al. 2016). In the United States, ART is currently recommended for all patients with HIV regardless of viral load or CD4 count (level of evidence AI “A1”)  (Dube MP. , Stein JH. 2018).

Prior to the third revolutionary step, patients with HIV had been left to wait until their immune systems had nearly failed. The rationalizations behind waiting included few available HIV medications earlier in the HIV pandemic, worry about developing drug resistance, and high cost of HIV medications. Earlier initiation of ART demonstrated the benefit of starting ART before 500 vs at 350 (Lundgren et al. 2015; O’Connor et al. 2017). Additional studies on the pathogenicity of related SIV seeding in rhesus monkeys (Whitney et al. 2014) and HIV seeding in humans (Abrahams et al. 2019; Henrich et al. 2017; Pankau et al. 2020) soon after infection justified limiting HIV spread within a patient’s body as early as possible. The added benefit of eliminating HIV transmission when viral loads are undetectable made rapid treatment initiation after HIV diagnosis – also known as test and treat (Garnett and Baggaley 2009) – the standard-of-care globally (Saag et al. 2018). A promising outcome of earlier ART initiation includes earlier ART recipients having more rapid decay in reservoir size over time (Massanella et al. 2021).

INtegrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) are currently a mainstay of many clinical guidelines (Ghosn et al. 2018). INSTIs are often first-line in the US, while in the European Union and France, INSTIs are among first-line agents, including tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafenamide (NRTIs) plus either rilpivirine (an NNRTI) or boosted darunavir (a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor). The WHO recommends an NNRTI-based strategy of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus emtricitabine (or lamivudine) plus efavirenz; dolutegravir or low-dose efavirenz are alternatives (World Health Organization 2016). The global trend favors the use of INSTIs (Ghosn et al. 2018). As such, it remains vitally important to anticipate how integrase resistance might develop.

A fourth revolution came as a shift in thinking about patients with HIV to include people at risk of acquiring HIV. Those at risk include people with occupational exposure, exposure after intimate partner violence, and exposure after other high-risk activities. High-risk activities included injection drug use or sex with PLWH before it was known that virally suppressed PLWHA were not high-risk sexual contacts for their serodiscordant sexual partners. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) was developed based on medications at low risk of drug resistance and quick bioavailability. Taken within 72 hours of potential exposure to HIV, cART such as emtricitabine and tenofovir protected against establishment of HIV infections (US Public Health Service 2017).

Insights from treatment as prevention (www.cdc.gov/hiv/risk/art/index.html) and PEP (www.cdc.gov/hiv/risk/pep/index.html) were extended to trials giving people at risk of acquiring HIV access to ART prophylactically PrEP (www.cdc.gov/hiv/risk/prep/index.html), before becoming infected with HIV.

docs.title: HIV-1 drug resistance
docs.text: Once HIV enters the body and establishes a persistent reservoir, the current best outcome for a patient is to achieve a functional cure with antiretroviral therapy (ART). The goal of ART is to achieve an undetectable HIV viral load. This is because decreased viral load is associated with improved immune function, as well as improved non-AIDS complications of HIV. While acquiring drug resistance can impact HIV viral fitness (Lloyd, Kent, and Winnall 2014), such resistance readily occurs in the context of no/inadequate ART or ART interruptions. As drugs against HIV started to come out in the early 90s, drug resistance began to develop. Earlier ART regimens were monotherapies, such as with zidovudine (AZT) alone. These were insufficient to prevent intrahost HIV replication and evolution. Drug resistance in 12 countries across the developing world is higher than 10% (Mega 2019). More worrisome still are reports of extensive multidrug resistant HIV in patients who have not used ART previously (Raymond et al. 2020).

docs.title: Chapter 2: How we know what we know about HIV
Abstract
docs.text:
What we know about HIV is directly tied to how we know what we know. In Chapter 2 I summarize select methods used in key papers throughout the past 40 years of HIV research. These methods were used to detect HIV, to measure HIV gene expression by way of mRNA or protein abundances, and to measure HIV sequence heterogeneity. Clinical interrogation of HIV information is also discussed. Points to consider:

  • how much information is recovered with a given method,

  • how many samples can be processed at a given time, and

  • how progressively newer methods improved on pervious methods.

docs.title: Introduction – reading HIV information
docs.text: The methods used to study HIV have changed drastically over the last 40 years since the first AIDS case report (CDC 1981). Progress came from parallel advances in both computing hardware, nucleic acid sequencing and computer software methods to analyze and handle progressively larger sequencing datasets. Details of the computational hardware side of these advances are outside the scope of this dissertation. Regarding nucleic acid sequencing, this time can be very roughly divided into pre-sequencing and post-sequencing eras. Protein sequencing falls outside of the scope of the present dissertation and so is not discussed.

docs.title: The pre-sequencing era of HIV informatics is marked by qualitative datasets
docs.text: The pre-sequencing era was a time around the discovery of HIV, but before the wide adoption of nucleic acid sequencing methods to directly interrogate experimental systems or clinical samples. However, it is important to understand that the major advances in the pre-sequencing era were founded on the growing availability of high-quality HIV-1 and related viral genomes. These were part of several disjointed HIV genome projects, and here these are explicitly called HIV sequencing projects, after the technical usage of a biological entity’s genome sequencing project (Shendure et al. 2017). Shortly after one of the first HIV genomes was stabilized as a molecular clone (Hahn et al. 1984), the first HIV-1 reference genome was completed in 1985 (Ratner et al. 1985). It is represented as either GenBank:K03455.1 or RefSeq:NC_001802.1. Lower-throughput qualitative assays were founded on this seminal HIV sequence information.

docs.title: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
docs.text:
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a method used to amplify targeted regions of DNA. It was one of the first molecular methods used to interrogate HIV as HIV proviral sequences. Most often, prior information is necessary to optimize each PCR. The user can select which sequences of DNA to amplify based off known sequence. Short (approximately 20 nucleotides long) homologous sequences in the forward and reverse orientation are used to prime DNA polymerization. These form a primer window, which allows for the amplification of everything between the ends of the inward facing primers and copying of the primer spanning region. This is analogous to a pair of binoculars which enable the user to view everything within the field of view, not including the black field of view taken up by the binoculars.

The advent of thermostable Taq (Saiki et al. 1988) and thermocyclers helped bring PCR into labs across the world. For his work and for inventing the PCR method, Kary B Mullis was awarded half of a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993. Benefits of PCR include sensitivity to detect low copy number target sequences, as well as specificity for sequences with homology to primers used. Limitations of PCR include if a target is in an area with extremely low or high GC content, which may hinder amplification. Example, GC-rich sequences do not amplify, while AT-rich sequences amplify (sometimes too) well. Areas with secondary structure may not amplify well, although this is not believed to be a major problem for most DNA sequences. PCR using commercially available kits can amplify ACGT-containing sequences because kits include dA, dC, dG, and dT. Base modifications like A methylation, C methylation or C hydroxymethylation are effectively erased when a target region is amplified. DNA damage might be overwritten, which may affect validity of downstream applications. The DNA polymerases used for PCR have an intrinsic fidelity and processivity. Fidelity in the context of a nucleic acid polymerase refers to how faithfully information encoded in a template is copied to newly synthesized strands. Procesivity refers to the ability of an enzyme to remain on its template, enabling continued synthesis. The first available DNA polymerases had lower fidelity and processivity, and these limited the ability to amplify sequences longer than 5-10 kilobase (kb). Newer polymerases can amplify DNA to >40kb. In contrast to cellular genomic DNA replication, in vitro DNA polymerases lack proofreading, and so they can introduce errors into sequences during PCR. Errors are subsequently amplified with progressive PCR cycles. While experiments can be designed around most of PCR’s limitations, such avoidance has precluded work vital to the study of HIV.

Nested PCR combines at least two pairs of primers approximating the target window to be amplified, and two sets of cycles to increase sensitivity of detecting specific analytes (Green and Sambrook 2019). This has been important for detecting HIV in clinical samples, especially in the context of antiretroviral therapy and low plasma viral load. Until relatively recently it was not tractable to amplify nearly full-length HIV. Newer protocols leveraging improved Taq and RT isoforms and nested PCR have redressed this successfully.

docs.title: Reverse transcription with reverse transcriptase (RT)
docs.text:
Importantly, PCR can efficiently amplify DNA targets. This is because DNA has less secondary structure compared to RNA. DNA is also less susceptible to degradation in normal laboratory conditions. Until recently, to sequence RNA, one needed to convert RNA to DNA. This was done with viral reverse transcriptase enzymes. The importance of this work was recognized as Howard Martin Temin, David Baltimore, and Renato Dulbecco split the Nobel prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1975 "for their discoveries concerning the interaction between tumor viruses and the genetic material of the cell." An important tumor virus studied was Moloney murine leukemia virus (MMLV), a retrovirus with reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymatic activity. Commercial RT has been mostly MMLV (Zucha et al. 2020). An important technical limitation of RT is the relatively high error rate compared to DNA polymerase in PCR. RT error rates in different viruses can vary between about 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100,000 (Menéndez-Arias 2009). cDNA made from RT could be subjected to subsequent PCR.

RT PCR protocols can differ, but they can generally be divided into two flavors: one-step and two-step. One-step combines RT with PCR in a single tube. Users must supply target-specific primers. This is better suited for detecting a single target from a given sample. Two-step RT PCR, which is better for detecting multiple targets in a sample, separates the RT step and the PCR step. Primers may include oligo-dT, random hexamer, or target-specific primers. Random primers can have more off-target amplification artifacts. RT qPCR (q is for “quantitative”) offered a semiquantitative improvement but is similarly limited by primer specificity which limits target sequence amplification.

These methods are all endpoint assays. The measurand is the intensity of a band or fluorescence at one or multiple timepoints. You never directly evaluate sequence info. Instead, you deduce sequence homology based on ability to detect amplification products at expected weights in absence of other non-specific bands. There remains no way to differentiate between a true positive and a false positive which happens to amplify near a given weight on a gel. qPCR is more sensitive, but remains an indirect endpoint assay.

docs.title: The post-sequencing era of HIV informatics is marked by quantitative datasets
docs.text:
The post-sequencing era is defined by the growing adoption of increasingly higher-throughput and cheaper sequencing methods to detect HIV across various sample matrices (e.g., plasma, venous blood, tissue), usually paired with mapping derivative sequences back to an HIV reference genome (HXB2). This is explicitly called resequencing (Shendure et al. 2017), and here I call it HIV resequencing v1.0 to distinguish this as work done prior to the advent of HIV Informatics. The post-sequencing era proceeded roughly sequentially:

  1. Pairing reverse transcription with PCR with short-read sequencing

  2. Pairing reverse transcription with PCR with multiplexed short-read sequencing

  3. Pairing reverse transcription with PCR with long-read sequencing (my work and others’)

  4. Pairing reverse transcription with PCR with multiplexed long-read sequencing (my work and others’)

In addition to basic and translational science, HIV sequence heterogeneity has also been used to track HIV transmission with emerging molecular epidemiology methods. HIV transmission was demonstrated in a forensic case by Metzker et al. 2002 (Metzker et al. 2002). Because of the risk of perpetrating HIV stigma, concern of community members about HIV criminalization by overextending scientific results has been expressed (https://www.aidsmap.com/news/jan-2021/molecular-hiv-surveillance-friend-or-foe).

docs.title: HIV expression in select HIV models
docs.text:
Measuring HIV is challenging due to HIV’s myriad forms, reviewed in Chapter 7 (Gener 2021b). “HIV gene expression” as a concept can be problematic because of the phrase’s relative ambiguity. Investigators might mean to describe abundance of HIV mRNA, HIV DNA, HIV protein. In this dissertation I focused on measuring HIV sequence information and/or HIV mRNA abundance.

Early work, for example Schwartz et al. elaborated important cell culture models for studying HIV mRNA expression. Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 HLtat cells (ARP-1293) are cells which stably express a truncated version of Tat, sometimes called Tat-1. (This will be revisited in Chapter 6 (Gener 2021a) with GENER13). This cell line was important to be able to easily study gene expression of proteins driven by the HIV-1 LTR promoter. Another cell line, Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 HLfB cells (ARP-1300) - (Hadzopoulou-Cladaras et al. 1989; Mermer et al. 1990) (https://www.hivreagentprogram.org/Catalog/cellBanks/ARP-1300.aspx) was used to demonstrate that mRNAs containing a Rev Response Element (RRE) (Chapter 1 Chapter 1 Figure 5: HIV-1 NL4-3 Rev Response element) were positively modulated by Rev protein. Products of non-RRE mRNAs were negatively regulated by Rev.

Transfecting cells (HeLa, CD4+ T cells, others) with HIV cDNA clones was a common way to study the effects of the first HIV proteins studied. A limitation of this approach was susceptibility of cloned mRNAs’ transcripts to additional splicing which might not be physiological. This highlights the difficulty in distinguishing between co-transcriptional and post-transcriptional splicing. I did not address this relationship in this dissertation, but it is relevant for the splicing patterns described in Chapter 6.

Once an HIV genome was available, primers could be designed to amplify and detect HIV. Such HIV PCR was more useful in experimental systems which began with infection of an HIV-negative sample with a known HIV strain, for example, NL4-3. Partly because of HIV’s inherent sequence variability, the use of PCR amplification to measure HIV in clinical samples was limited. Other considerations include fidelity and processivity of both RT and DNA polymerases used in RT PCR, as well as the availability and cost of sequencing methods.

docs.title: HIV tropism
docs.text: Methods used to study HIV tropism in vitro include cell culture and HIV infection determined by reverse transcriptase activity, p24 antigen detection, and PCR. Methods used to study HIV tropism in vivo included immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization. (Table 3.8 (Levy 2007)). Importantly, sequencing has only recently been used to follow HIV across different potential reservoirs.

docs.title: Clinical HIV testing
docs.text:
While the detailed clinical management of HIV/AIDS patients falls outside the scope of this dissertation, HIV diagnosis is within the scope of HIV information. As such, I will describe how HIV diagnostics and monitoring have developed and relate them back to the kinds of information measured in more basic studies of HIV.

Pre-sequencing era tests relied on a patient’s immune responses to HIV by detecting a patient’s humoral responses in the form of antibodies against HIV antigens, and later incorporated detection of HIV antigens. Prior to addition of p24, tests in the context of AIDS were more likely to be false negative. This was because immunosuppressed patients sometimes lost their antibody responses.

Sequencing is not generally used for HIV diagnosis. However, HIV mRNA information is assayed during HIV treatment. These areas of overlap include viral load measurement (which is not sequencing) and HIV genotyping (which is sequencing).

docs.title: Development of diagnostic HIV testing
docs.text:
Concurrent with the isolation of a putative AIDS-causing virus (Barré-Sinoussi et al. 1983; Gallo et al. 1983) and the naming of HIV (AP 1986), there was high demand for an “AIDS test” for at least a couple of reasons. One was to diagnose AIDS in patients to prevent the spread of the AIDS virus. Another was to protect healthcare systems’ blood supplies from contamination. A clinical test for AIDS based on measuring analytes would ultimately never be developed because of the need to integrate acute clinical information with a patient’s past medical history to ascertain a patient’s risk factor(s) for acquiring HIV with measurable analyte(s). However, tests could be developed for an AIDS virus (Alexander 2016).

Once the biomedical community realized that such a deadly bloodborne pathogen could be transmitted in unscreened blood/blood products, there was an immediate need to screen pooled blood/blood products for the AIDS-causing virus. Tests were developed to screen pooled blood/blood products. They worked by detecting antibodies against immobilized HIV antigens. These first assays were sensitive, but not specific. While there were some false positives, the benefit of removing contaminated blood products outweighed the harm of delivering a false positive to a patient at risk of acquiring AIDS. Positive results were given to blood donors, and these people were prohibited from future donations. Since the first HIV tests were not clinical tests, physicians could not order them for their patients at risk of developing or suspected of having AIDS. At that time there was no treatment for HIV to prevent AIDS, however some AIDS-defining conditions could be treated.

HIV diagnostic tests were developed, progressing through multiple iterations. The first iterations focused on detecting HIV-1 M B HTLV-III/HXB2/LAV sequence only, then HIV-2 was added, and next HIV-2 and HIV-1 O. Today, fourth-generation enzyme immunoassays detect antibodies and HIV-1 p24 antigen. Alternative testing includes rapid third-generation enzyme immunoassays that detect antibodies only (Ghosn et al. 2018). Rapid tests are lateral flow assays which give results in 10-20 minutes, and can be done practically anywhere (as opposed to in the confines of a lab). Other assays require specialized equipment running multiple samples a a time and can only be done in specialized labs. A shortcoming of rapid HIV tests is an inability to detect HIV during the acute phase before sufficient production of antibodies (Ghosn et al. 2018). While 4th generation assays are more expensive, their utility in at risk populations can justify their use. Serology and antigen detection is generally preferred for screening adults. In the context of neonatal HIV diagnosis and need for viral load as diagnosis instead. This is because of maternal anti-HIV antibodies for the first several months postpartum which might be detected as false positive neonate. In 2006, the CDC recommended that HIV testing be considered as part of routine care (Alexander 2016).

docs.title: HIV viral load
docs.text:
HIV viral load (VL) is used for initial assessment after HIV diagnosis in adults and for subsequence monitoring. VL is generally not used for adult or pediatric HIV diagnosis. However, VL is used in newborn HIV diagnosis. Current methods to measure HIV viral load are diverse, reviewed elsewhere (Ginocchio 2001). TaqMan probes are used for some VL assays. These probes can tolerate some heterogeneity, and until recently have been a preferred method to determine HIV VL in clinical samples. PCR may also be used. Sequencing is generally not used to assess VL. Commercial HIV VL assays are generally specific for HIV-1 (Dube MP. , Stein JH. 2018).

HIV VL is important for initial assessment because 1.) a patient's pre-ART viral load level and 2.) the magnitude of viral load decline after initiation of ART both provide prognostic information about the probability of disease progression (Murray et al. 1999). Decreases in HIV VL after initiating antiretroviral therapy were associated with decreased risk of progression to AIDS (Marschner et al. 1998; Murray et al. 1999; Thiébaut et al. 2000).

docs.title: HIV Genotyping
docs.text:
In resource-rich settings, one of the first things that is done after a person is diagnosed with HIV is that ART drug resistance profiling is ordered. This is usually done by way of virus (HIV) genotyping. Genotypic resistance testing may be used to stage HIV disease and to assist in the selection of ART regimens (Dube MP. , Stein JH. 2018). (Grading scheme: Strength of Recommendation + Quality of Evidence for Recommendation. AII “A2”, where A is Strong recommendation for the statement; and 2 or II is “One or more well-designed, non-randomized trials or observational cohort studies with long-term clinical outcomes”. HIV genotyping is indicated prior to treatment initiation or change, treatment failure, if ART initiation is delayed, or if genotyping is otherwise clinically indicated. (https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/table/table-3-laboratory-testing-schedule-monitoring-people-hiv-and-after-initiation-antiretroviral) (Dube MP. , Stein JH. 2018). Genotyping is based on sequencing cDNA from RT PCR of partial HIV-1 pol, (PR, RT) and more recently complete pol (PR + RT + IN).

HIV genotyping has its limitations and advantages. To be successful at HIV genotyping, there must be enough HIV mRNA analyte in the sample matrix. This usually means HIV RNA levels greater than 500 to 1,000 copies/mL. Otherrwise, viral amplification for resistance testing may not be successful (BII).” Source: https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/guidelines/adult-and-adolescent-arv/baseline-evaluation?view=full (Dube MP. , Stein JH. 2018). Access to sequencing facilities in many settings currently limits the implementation of HIV genotyping clinically. When Sanger sequencing is used, Sanger is known to be insensitive to variants occurring less than 10-20% of the time (https://aidsinfo.nih.gov/guidelines/html/1/adult-and-adolescent-arv/6/drug-resistance-testing). An advantage of Sanger though is relative cheap cost per sample when processed one at a time (as opposed to multiplexed with NGS/2nd generation sequencing or 3rd generation sequencing). Limitations from PCR include primers biasing resistance profiling to the window of observation between the primers. Variations on PCR including nested PCR are often used to amplify HIV sequences for sequencing. Because HIV exhibits formidable sequence heterogeneity even over relatively conserved regions in its genome, the use of PCR primers selects against sequences which differ markedly from primer-complimentary sequences. As mentioned before, a nontrivial consideration for HIV genotyping is sequencing samples with sufficient analytes (HIV genome equivalents) to yield sequence. Acute cases of HIV infection generally have more than enough HIV to recover sequence. Chronic cases of HIV may or may not depending on the amount of latency in the patient when sampled. Other potential PCR concerns of GC bias are not immediately relevant for HIV-1, because the average GC content across the HIV genome approximates that seen in the host genome (Gener, unpublished). Proviral DNA testing is performed rarely (source: https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/table/table-3-laboratory-testing-schedule-monitoring-people-hiv-and-after-initiation-antiretroviral) (Dube MP. , Stein JH. 2018).

An important consideration in NGS-based HIV genotyping is the risk of averaging out HIV heterogeneity for the sake of a complete genome assembly. Often, consensus sequences derived from individual patient samples collected at a given time are provided, and variants are called for subsequence resistance analyses (e.g., comparing to the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance database). Reads mapping to a region might be filtered out if they don’t contribute to the most common sequences. These might still represent viable virus subpopulations which may contribute to a patient’s HIV drug resistance. This limitation can be redressed by applying a second mapping step after the first assembly to collect secondary variability.

Treatment success for first-line ART is defined as reaching undetectable viral load by 48 weeks after ART initiation, where undetectable is defined as a plasma viral load below 50 copies per mL (Ghosn et al. 2018). Functionally, sustained viral loads <200 copies per mL are another commonly used threshold.

docs.title: Writing HIV information
docs.text:
It is important to note that cloning each of the first 9 HIV gene products (Gag, Gag-Pol as Pol, Vif, Vpr, Vpu, Env, Nef, and spliced Tat and Rev) and subsequent drug and vaccine development began during the pre-sequencing era. Efforts generally did not consider additional HIV sequence heterogeneity beyond the initial information in HXB2-like HIV-1s. A notable exception was when considering resistance to fusion inhibitor maraviroc, which is limited to HIV patients with R5-tropic HIV-1s, which is often seen earlier during the natural course of infection (see Chapter 1). Another exception included the discovery and concurrent justification of HIV’s 10th gene product: antisense protein (Cassan et al. 2016). In that study, an open reading frame (ORF) which appeared to be a relatively new addition to some HIV-1 M group B subgroup strains was noted.

HIV RT generated HIV cDNA which could be cloned into bacterial or other expression vectors. Attention to promoter selection and codon optimization in the case of protein expression in non-mammalian systems was necessary. The availability of more and more restriction enzymes over time increased the ability of molecular biologists to manipulate HIV clones. As such, the synthetic clone NL4-3 has become a molecular biology staple and is still commonly used in lentivirus vectors and mammalian expression vectors. An issue with HIV-based plasmids is the repetitive LTR sequences bordering the internal HIV genes. These repetitive regions offer E. coli the opportunity to excise internal sequences while preserving resistance cassettes, for example, the beta lactamase ORF on the NL4-3 backbone. Engineered bacterial strains able to carry repetitive elements like LTRs have enabled easier cloning. New approaches like CRISPR/Cas9 have showed promise in the case of manipulating HIV in vitro an in vivo (Dash et al. 2019; Kaminski et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2016; Yin et al. 2017).
