docs.title: Chapter 3: HIV Informatics is a framework to advance the study of HIV
Abstract
docs.text:
We kept HIV/AIDS in check over the past 40 years by continuing to learn about HIVs: the previously unknown viruses found to cause AIDS. In Chapter 1 we saw how HIV information in the nucleic acid space shifts between HIV RNA in the HIV virion and HIV-infected cells to HIV DNA as unintegrated cDNA and integrated provirus. We also saw how the number of HIV sequences has grown, and how drugs were developed based on sequencing of one of the first HIV-1 isolates HXB2 and/or on in vitro work with a closely related synthetic HIV-1 lab strain NL4-3. In Chapter 2 we saw that HIV tests were eventually designed to detect HIV in clinical samples. Experimental model systems (some reviewed briefly in Chapter 2) were developed to push progress without the need to wait for more human HIV cases. Cell culture systems predominated, and then animal models were developed. A major take-home from these first two chapters is that progress has been directly tied to being able to extract HIV information from relevant systems, to dissect the parts of the virus, and to study these in culture. Later sequencing studies supported putative molecular HIV targets.

People living with HIV AIDS (PLWHA) are living longer thanks in part to their HIV treatments (Alejandro R Gener 2021). The HIV/AIDS research community has since dissected presumably all the functional parts of the HIV genome by isolating parts with available molecular cloning and sequencing methods. However, despite all this progress, general problems remain to be solved by the HIV research community. New methods revealed HIV establishes itself in multiple tissues with unknown long-term health consequences. It remains unclear to what extent findings in model systems are relevant to human health. Drug resistance is an emerging problem for people at risk of acquiring HIV or with problems getting access to and/or staying linked to care. Therefore, there remains a need to continue the study of HIV to anticipate its effects on human health and to counter its natural abilities to evolve resistance to current treatments.

Past progress was made by separate groups working in parallel. However, after 35+ years we still do not have a vaccine for HIV. We still do not have a sterilizing cure to flush HIV from HIV patients’ bodies without risking viral reactivation and secondary drug resistance. While these goals are not the subject of this dissertation work, the study of HIV as a means of achieving these goals is. Now that we have better tools and analytical methods to describe sequence heterogeneity, it serves to reason that it is important to revisit past assumptions about HIV, and to develop more comprehensive approaches to recover HIV information (little “i”) from HIV samples. Chapter 3 introduces HIV Informatics (big “I”), a new framework to approach HIV information in the context of HIV sequence variability across HIV’s diverse forms with the goal of enabling investigators and clinicians to maximize the information gained from their assays.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
To satisfy Koch’s Postulates was to isolate a putatively pathogenic organism in sick and only sick individuals, to grow this organism under standardized conditions, and then to reinfect healthy hosts with these putative disease-causing organisms. Viruses including HIV are not technically organisms because they are not alive. Instead, they are replicative sets of genes which depend on infecting permissive cells to enable their full replication cycle. As such, Koch’s Postulates were problematic for HIV/AIDS. At the time AIDS was noticed and a putative virus identified, it remained unknown which cell types could maintain HIV in culture.

Early work in 1983 provided some evidence that a new reverse-transcribing virus might have been the primary cause of AIDS (Barré-Sinoussi et al. 1983; Gallo et al. 1983). Thankfully, experimentation on humans with lethal infectious agents was precluded by research community members observing contemporary bioethical norms (E.g. Nuremberg Code). With a virus as a likely culprit, a goal was to describe the complete genome of a representativ AIDS virus isolate, possibly one of the ones already growing in one of the first few labs studying putative AIDS viruses (e.g., LAV, HTLV-III, BRU, etc.). This would have served to enable diagnostic tests for the virus in people, to screen blood-derived products, and to possibly develop anti-AIDS virus medications. Researchers tried to stabilize HIV with available molecular techniques, including using lambdaphage to some success (Hahn et al. 1984). An HIV-1 isolate was finally stabilized as a provirus plasmid clone pHXB-2D (Fisher et al. 1985). Freezing HIV as DNA as opposed to propagating it over successive passages prevented HIV’s rapid evolution in culture, facilitating HIV’s study. This event enabled labs around the world to study parts of the virus, to develop diagnostic tests, and most importantly for HIV, to develop targeted pharmaceuticals after initial trial and error (National Institute of Allergy and Infectiour Disease 2018).

An assumption before beginning my dissertation work was that we had described all relevant parts of the HIV genome, including the HIV genome’s organization. At the time it was reasonable to believe we had described all the relevant parts of HIV. What’s more, we had drugs that worked. We eventually achieved over the first 30 years of HIV/AIDS research a functional cure for HIV. We can prevent people with HIV from becoming AIDS patients by diagnosing HIV sooner, linking patients to care sooner, and keeping them engaged in care. We even treat people exposed to HIV prophylactically with post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and treat people at risk of acquiring HIV with antiretroviral therapy in the form of preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP). However, stepping back from the field’s progress, these gains were made with now quite dated methods. HIV drug resistance is an emerging problem in undiagnosed people and when people have difficulty adhering to their therapy. It remains vital to anticipate HIV’s adaptability. To best ensure success, we must make sure we understand HIV biology maximally, focusing on the known parts of the virus which we believe we have resolved, while being open to new knowledge from overlooked viral features.

We now know that most reverse-transcribing viruses like HIV exhibit high sequence variability (Menéndez-Arias 2009). This presents the HIV research community with unique challenges which were only recently able to be addressed. One challenge with the traditional approach to genome sequencing is made especially apparent when trying to describe heterogeneous HIV genomes between and within patients. In a kind of genomic (as opposed to molecular) Koch’s postulates, investigators would strive to describe the genome of a first representative organism or viral isolate. They would do this by sequencing a sample with available methods, and then use de novo genome assembly methods to build a new genome. This would be the organism’s (or virus’) genome sequencing project, and the result would hopefully be at least one reference genome. Once this singular reference genome was available, all subsequent sequencing experiments and other molecular biology methods would be based on the foundation of this reference. These subsequent experiments are sometimes called resequencing, where samples are sequenced and then mapped to a preexisting reference. However, that approach tacitly ignores biological variability between individuals. An interesting point to note is that many scientists unfamiliar with the progress of genomics often fail to distinguish between sequencing and resequencing experiments. The result of these failures serves to obscure the biological variability between the samples being sequenced, such as HIV viruses between patients, or HIV virions within a given patient. An example of how HIV information is ignored for simplicity’s sake is how HIV drugs have been designed. These are often based on crystal structures of HIV isolates, such as from HXB2 or NL4-3. Drugs are not designed with HIV heterogeneity in mind, with unknown clinical consequences.

docs.title: HIV information as a knowledge set
docs.text: As with any modern science, the study of HIV carries with it an easy to overlook epistemological dilemma. While we have learned a lot about HIV, how do we know if what we know about HIV is both true and comprehensive. How do we know whether that is all that is to be known about a given aspect of HIV? If knowledge is a justified true belief, what can we make of HIV information? This can be abstracted as a set described by a US public servant and unlikely philosophical reference, the late Donald Rumsfeld. He proposed a set of three kinds of information: known knowns, known unknowns, and unknown unknowns. I adapt these divisions for HIV below.

docs.title: HIV’s known knowns
docs.text: The HIV literature is assumed to be true. In practice there are limitations to this unlikely possibility. It is impractical for any scientist studying HIV to know everything ever published about HIV. Modern seekers of HIV information are limited by their bandwidth but aided by the experience and the expertise of others who have studied HIV longer. Ancillary sciences, such as other virologies, bioinformatics, animal genetics provide support for rough frameworks to think about how HIV might interact with the human body. Besides the shear amount of information, past information was acquired through the lenses of lower-throughput methods which effectively limited their scope.

docs.title: HIV’s known unknowns
docs.text: Current HIV researchers have prioritized certain areas to test hypotheses. Priorities include Cure Science, and HIV Vaccines. For example, some of us think vaccines may work to protect against contracting HIV, but we don’t yet know which vaccine(s) will work, or whether the sequence heterogeneity inherent to the HIV replication cycle preclude HIV from ever having an efficacious vaccine. While we don’t know exactly why past vaccines have failed, we can measure improvement with progressive iterations of development. Current vaccines in trials are better than the first HIV vaccines. This is in part due to integrating knowledge about HIV virion structure, requirements of host cells for antigen presentation, and other improvements in vaccine development.

docs.title: HIV’s unknown unknowns
docs.text:
These includes areas such as HIV weak spots which are unknown to HIV scientists and clinicians. They might constitute the next therapeutic avenues for antiretroviral treatment, or redress systemic limitations which had not been previously appreciated. These are easy to see in hindsight. For example, the cost of HIV medications was untenable for use in the developing world, but subsequent partnerships between pharmaceutical companies and governments to guarantee access to lower- and middle-income countries to affordable antiretroviral therapies. Before we knew HIV had druggable targets, AIDS patients were at the mercy of clinical empiricism, which cost millions of lives. With current therapeutic progress, focus has logically shifted from finding treatments that work to identifying people living with undiagnosed HIV/AIDS (PLWHA), and getting medicines out to PLWHA to prevent onset of AIDS and non-AIDS HIV-associated diseases. However, there are still 40 million PLWHA. Drug resistance is a perpetually emergent problem (Raymond et al. 2020). These raise the questions: what else is there to HIV biology? What did we miss? What can be improved?

While practitioners of the modern scientific method may pride themselves as empirical agents, in practice much of modern science is steeped in tradition and serendipity. Referencing big names and faithfully believing dogma are two areas where modern science falls short of ideal. In practice, this often translates to assumptions that are rarely challenged. A quirk of the modern scientific method is the constant evolution of technologies to aid scientists’ pursuit of knowledge. With new methods, it often pays to revisit past experiments, and the assumptions we take for granted. Because of HIV’s many nuances, it remains important to implement new approaches considering prior knowledge, and ideally identifying assumptions to retest for validity. With that, HIV Informatics is a framework unifying HIV models, nucleic acid (re)sequencing, bioinformatics, and validation to maximize the HIV information gained from assays.

docs.title: Bioinformatics
docs.text:
The US National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) defines bioinformatics as a subdiscipline overlapping biology and computer science. Bioinformatics deals with the acquisition, storage, analysis, and dissemination of biological data. Bioinformaticians use and/or develop computer programs for a range of applications, and establishing evolutionary relationships. Such relationships can provide insights into biological functions of whole genes, or parts of genes called domains (protein) or features/elements (nucleic acids). The most common forms of such data are sequences of biopolymers deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid (DNA and RNA) and proteins, which are first determined and subsequently stored in a variety of data file formats in large publicly accessible databases. An analogy for bioinformatics is determining the linguistic rules of genomes.

For the study of HIV, the availability of an HIV reference genome allowed for the molecular definition of this pathogen, and catalyzed subsequent dissection by molecular cloning, in vitro and in vivo functional studies on identified viral proteins, and identification of new antiviral agents for most if not all the identified steps in the HIV replication cycle. We now have a functional cure for HIV comprised of validated combinations of the above HIV drugs thanks to informed studies after the isolation of the pathogen, genome sequencing, and information dissemination to the broader scientific community. This required the input of thousands of investigators, including many of the forerunners of HIV bioinformaticians. Work is ongoing.

HIV’s genomic content fluctuates between RNA as in HIV virions and DNA as linear cDNA in the preintegration complexes, circularized unintegrated cDNA, and integrated DNA in HIV proviruses (reviewed in the introduction of Chapter 7 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021)). This can be simplified as two analyte targets: HIV DNA and HIV RNA. Of the two, DNA is generally more stable because of fewer environmental DNAses, and has been easier to work with in the lab. Until recently, one of the most common ways to recover HIV information from RNA samples with HIV sequence had been to use commercially prepared recombinant reverse transcriptase in reverse transcription kits to make relatively more stable HIV cDNA, often paired with polymerase chain reaction to amplify regions of interest. This is unfortunately called RNA-seq, despite not actually sequencing HIV RNA. In the case of proviral integration, the most common approaches generate DNA amplicons. So, a common bottleneck for recovering information from HIV samples has been DNA sequencing (DNA-seq).

HIV information is stored in different places for different purposes. Primary sequencing data with associated metadata is available in the Short-Read Archive (SRA) at the US National Center for Biotechnology Information/National Library of Medicine/National Institutes of Health (NCBI/NLM/NIH). Processed data is available in GEO, with some functional overlap with SRA. Other NCBI databases include GenBank for primary assembled and annotated nucleic acid and peptide sequence, RefSeq for expert-curated assembled and annotated genomes. A new database, the Third-Party Annotation database stores sequences based on previously available sequence entries with the addition of new changes or annotations that are evidence-based. The European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) serves a similar purpose, by providing functional redundancy with NCBI resources. In the case of HIV there is also the Los Alamos National Laboratory’s HIV Databases, including the HIV Sequence Database, and HIV Molecular Immunology Database. While RefSeq entries are generally considered to be a gold standard set of reference genomes, the HIV Sequence Database is viewed as the gold standard for HIV genomics. Large funding organizations and a growing number of journals often require investigators to establish a data-sharing plan to ensure that data generated in the pursuit of publicly funded research is deposited permanently in accessible forms to enable rigor and reproducibility in research. These databases are where public data are stored.

After the first HIV strains were isolated and grown in culture, one of these was cloned and sequenced as a reference genome (Fisher et al. 1985). To determine how conserved HIV sequences were to each other, more and more sequences have been collected over time (See figure in Chapter 1). Tangential to the need to molecularly dissect the parts of HIV, it became apparent that HIV information could be used to follow HIV transmission. This was useful information for public health measures. These two branches of HIV informatics (virology and molecular epidemiology) have only recently fused in the form of HIV genotyping assays, thanks in large part to: 1.) cheaper sequencing, 2.) better bioinformatics support, 3.) validated clinical assays.

docs.title: Sequencing vs. Resequencing
docs.text:
Biomolecule sequencing can be roughly divided into nucleic acid and protein sequencing (Shendure et al. 2017). Of the two nucleic acids, the development of DNA sequencing methods came first. These methods were used to define and grow the genome space of species ranging from precellular reproductive entities like viruses, viroids, and organelles to members of the known kingdoms of life.

Priority for genome sequencing projects came by identifying presumably representative organisms and defining a presumably representative genome. Because of limitations of earlier methods, the genomic material of multiple individuals was usually pooled to provide enough physical material to generate libraries for sequencing. This is called ensemble sequencing. Before cheaper higher throughput methods were available, larger genomes were sometimes built as patchworks of multiple individuals (for example, the original human genome draft).

DNA sequencing

The goal of genome sequencing projects was to provide as a deliverable at least one representative reference genome for a species. For smaller genomes, such as HIV, this was provided as HXB2 (K03455.1) and the RefSeq entry NC-001802.1. This is complicated by a lack of cloned HXB2 as a plasmid for use making HXB2 virus preparations. In part, that was due to known errors in the sequence which prevented more efficient replication. Comparative genomics using early HIV-1 sequences lead to the development of the currently most widely used HIV-1 lab strain, NL4-3 (Gener et al. 2021).

Interrogation of HIV in the nucleic acid space is usually bound by a reference genome. This is problematic with natural infections (as we’ll see in Chapter 9). A previous solution was to amplify env or pol, but at the expense of biasing results. You cannot see what fails to amplify.

docs.title: Models (models of HIV genome at different stages of replication, my graphical abstract slide)
docs.text: Many of the assumptions about models used to study HIV are based on historical methods used and/or lack of additional observational validation after the advent of newer methods.

docs.title: The HIV genome is generally modeled in two forms: virus and provirus.
docs.text: In Chapter 1 I covered that most HIV investigators think of mature HIV virions as being diploid, having two copies of coding/forward/positive/sense mRNA. This mRNA is polyadenylated near the end of the 3’ R. I described the genomic organization of HIV virion in Chapter 1 Figure. The HIV sequence database uses a proviral representation of the HIV-1 HXB2 genome, Genbank:K03455.1. The RefSeq entry for HIV uses a viral representation of the HIV-1 HXB2 genome, RefSeq:NC_001802.1. There is no standard format for displaying HIV genomes or for annotating HIV information content.

docs.title: The total number of HIV-1’s protein-coding genes has been assumed to be solved as 10.
docs.text:
Most HIV investigators will agree that there are at least 9 protein-coding HIV-1 genes. These are gag, pol, vif, vpr, vpu, env, nef, tat, rev. Tat and Rev are considered spliced as their mature forms. Some of the genes encode larger open reading frames (ORFs) encoding polyproteins which exhibit distinct forms between cells newly expressing HIV mRNA and immature virion, and mature virion which includes proteolytically cleaved final forms. The HIV polyproteins are cleaved by viral protease (Gag and Pol), or by host proteases (Env). Gag is cleaved by HIV protease into p17, p24, p7, p1, p2, p6. Pol is cleaved by HIV protease into protease/aspartyl peptidase (PR), p51 subunit of reverse transcriptase, p66 subunit of reverse transcriptase with an RNAse H domain, and integrase (IN). Env is cleaved by host proteases into gp120 and gp41. A 10th protein-coding HIV-1 gene was proposed in 1988 (Miller 1988), and further studies provided evolutionary information supporting its emergence as a recent regularly seen protein product in certain M group B subgroup HIV-1s (Cassan et al. 2016).

Newer interpretations of the organization of HIV genome consider Gag and Gag-Pol instead of Gag and Pol, as Pol has not been shown to be able to be made as a primary translation product. Gag-Pol is instead made from a frameshift that adds Pol-encoded amino acids prematurely onto the end of Gag at a ribosomal slippage site.

docs.title: Physical HIV virus models
docs.text: NL4-3 is the most common lab strain of HIV-1 (Gener et al. 2021). If a virus’ replication machinery maintained perfect sequence fidelity, as in a carbon-copy of each viral genome between generations, then it would make sense to use the virus produced after infection for subsequent infections. However, HIV RT is highly error prone. Repeating virus replications using stock from primary infected cells would generate progressively divergent viruses with each subsequent generation. Therefore, HIV is not normally maintained as a virus stock. It is maintained in a stabilized form as a plasmid or molecular clone, pNL4-3. Other stabilized HIV strains each have their own HIV-encoded plasmids.

docs.title: Cell lines
docs.text:
A limiting factor for the study of HIV early on was the availability of cell lines able to sustain HIV viral replication. One requirement of these first cell models was the need to be susceptible to HIV infection. Primary human patient and/or donor-derived peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were used to study transient infection. PBMCs are enriched for CD4+ T cells, which were among the first tissues used to study HIV. They were a prime target, as CD4+ T cell depletion was identified early in the study of the pathogenesis of HIV-associated immune deficiency. Early in the study of HIV, the study of CD4 pathogenesis took precedence. Later, macrophages were identified to be a susceptible to HIV

A problem with infecting primary cells is that cells would last only about 2 days once viral replication was activated (Wei et al. 1995). This isn’t unique to primary cells, but it precluded the use of establishing cell lines stably expressing HIV mRNAs and proteins. That said, some latently infected cell lines were created. Notable examples include U1 Jurkat and ACTH2 cells.

Eventually, several animal models were generated to study chronically infected tissues. These animals had similar development to human tissues, and could recapitulate gross disease as in the case of the Tg26 HIV transgenic mouse (Dickie et al. 1991). However, these mice lacked human immune systems, and so their utility studying HIV’s effects on the immune system were limited. For immune system studies, non-human primates were employed to varying degrees of success. Lastly, samples from natural infections were incidentally available. These samples are harder to come by with the advent of improved standards of care for people living with HIV/AIDS.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
If science is the empirical pursuit of knowledge, and knowledge is justified true believe, then the resources we use in our experiments can be considered propositions. The validity of an experiment which uses reagents is directly tied to the truthfulness of the state of such reagents. For example, if a sample of HIV-1 is defective, and a scientist uses the defective reagent with a new pharmaceutical compound they are testing for antiviral activity, the result of an inhibition assay might suggest incorrectly that the test compound has antiviral activity. Instead, in this example, the defective virus contributed to a false result. There are many reagents that are used routinely across biomedical science. Some reagents, such as those organized by the AIDS Reagent Program (ARP), are unique to HIV.

To mitigate potentially expensive mistakes, funding agencies like the NIH now require that key reagents be validated. This means that investigators should not simply trust the source of their reagents. In practice, this level of validation in not always implemented.

Ways HIV reagents are validated are from the manufacturers, and ideally once in the receiving lab. Reagents should also regularly be tested for performance, because some reagents (for example, molecular biology enzymes) may be compromised after years of freeze-thaws. As mentioned above, the ARP is one place where HIV researchers can go to for validated resources. That said, resources validation is not perfect. As we will see in Chapter 5 of this dissertation, key reagents can exhibit marked variability. Forms of validation for HIV include plasmid maps and sequences if a plasmid or virus stock is involved. If the reagent is an antibody, example immunoblots may be provided in good-faith. The current gold standard for plasmid validation is plasmid sequencing and assembly, often provided by a sequencing core at Center for Computational & Integrative Biology DNA Core at Massachusetts General Hospital. Addgene is a newer molecular biology repository which maintains some HIV-related plasmids and lentiviruses.

Tangential to reagent validation, it is important to Cross-validate findings in one related system to another. For example, results in one system should be consistent in others. If viruses derived from NL4-3 may behave the same, then this similarity should be able to be observed if true (as we will see in Chapter 8).

docs.title: Cautionary tales
docs.text:
The following are examples of how HIV information may be misconstrued.

Antibodies against consensus sequences

An example of what can go wrong with HIV information is illustrated by the availability of antibodies designed against HIV consensus sequences. Consensus sequences summarize the nucleic or amino acid sequence information. They are made after aligning multiple sequences to each other, and as such their accuracy are dependent on the algorithm(s) used to perform the multisequence alignment, as well as the accuracy and number of input sequences. A limitation for multisequence alignment includes poor ability to handle structural variants. An important, often overlooked, detail is that consensus sequences are NEVER real. Using a consensus sequence in place of a directly observed observation like an HIV genome assembly from a patient runs the risk of erasing variant linkage information between variants in the sequence and propagating an assumption about a sequence’s identity that is not true. It is rarely appropriate to use HIV consensuses in place of HIV isolates, directly assembled genomes. In practice, genome assembly may resemble the consensus process. However, each assembly is made relative to a given patient and/or sample. Consensus sequences can summarize information across thousands or more sequences, and a s consequence much sequence information is lost.

Antibodies are soluble B-cell receptors which are expressed in most mammals such as humans and mice after exposure to an immunogenic antigen. Of the 4 macromolecules, proteins are most likely to stimulate immune responses, and are thus immunogenic. Epitopes are the physical structure, often a short ~10 amino acid sequence, that an antibody binds to. Specific binding occurs when an antibody recognizes an epitope that was used to immunize the producer animal (e.g., a mouse). These kinds of interactions are generally specific. However, off-target binding may bind to similar shapes with distinct peptide sequences. Generally, sequence divergence beyond 1-2 amino acids is not well-tolerated, and target recognition may suffer. There are notable examples of single amino acid changes drastically decreasing binding affinity between targets. A classic example is taught in immunology courses: hen egg-whit lysozyme and antibody D1.3 (Murphy, Travers, and Walport 2008).

The most common lab strain of HIV-1 is NL4-3, with Nef protein sequence:

>HIV-1_NL4-3_nef

MGGKWSKSSVIGWPAVRERMRRAEPAADGVGAVSRDLEKHGAITSSNTAANNAACAWLEAQEEEEVGFPVTPQVPLRPMTYKAAVDLSHFLKEKGGLEGLIHSQRRQDILDLWIYHTQGYFPDWQNYTPGPGVRYPLTFGWCYKLVPVEPDKVEEANKGENTSLLHPVSLHGMDDPEREVLEWRFDSRLAFHHVARELHPEYFKNC*

Antibodies against Nef have been used to measure Nef protein levels across many different assays. Inspection of HIV-1 Nef antibodies available through the AIDS Reagent program revealed four HIV-1 Nef monoclonal antibodies. One of those, JR6 (ab42358, Abcam), was a mouse monoclonal antibody made from "ARELHPEYYKD". This is also called clone 01-009. Abcam cites 9 papers that have used this antibody (Lee et al. 2018):

Consensus antibodies might have utility in clinical samples where one does not know what the input HIV-1 Nef sequence may be, necessitating a fuzzy match. This remains a predominant method employed for detecting HIV proteins in patient-derived and/or clinical samples. However, use of an antibody distinct from the target in an experimental system is not advised. It is unclear whether the sources citing the use of this antibody we able to correctly identify Nef in their NL4-3 samples using antibodies against “ARELHPEYYKD”. The underlined portion is the difference between NL4-3 and HIV-1 M B Consensus (LANL HIV Database). Recall from Chapter 1 that NL4-3 is supposed to be a simple chimera between NY5 and LAV. For historical reasons, it’s difficult to distinguish between HXB2, IIIB, BRU, and LAV. These are treated nearly synonymously. Unfortunately, with the exception of pHXB2_D which we revalidated, these other strains do not exist as replication-competent plasmids for additional validation.

A search in LANL HIV Sequence Database for HIV-1/SIVcpz Nef returned 25 sequences. (Alignment type: Consensus/Ancestral; Year: 2004; Organism: HIV-1/SIVcpz; DNA/Protein: Protein; Region: nef; Subtype: ALL; Format: FASTA; Alignment ID: 104CP5; Number of sequences: 25. Accessed on 7/15/21.) Of those, 7 contained “ARELHPEYYKD”. This is believed to be identical to ARP-1539 (6.2). ARP-1539 was made using the HIV-1 M B subtype consensus, and ARP claims that the antibody exhibits activity against A, B, and C subtype Nefs. However, there is considerable heterogeneity of Nef protein sequences Across those subtypes. Other Nef antibodies include:

  • ARP-709, HIV-1 IIIB Nef (AE6) “VARELHPEYFKNC”. Per ARP, “The critical binding residue ARP-709 is the "N" in the IIIB C-terminal "YFKNC" sequence. This antibody does not react with HIV-1 SF2 nef.” This suggests that the c-terminal sequence is important for epitope recognition and antibody function.

  • ARP-1124, (AG11) has the same epitope as ARP-709.

  • ARP-3689 (EH1) “MARELHPEYYKDC”. Per ARP, “ARP-3689 recognizes SF2 and BRU Nef by radioimmunoprecipitation, western blot, and immunofluorescence assay.”

While ARP-709, ARP-1124, ARP-3689 have c-termini identical to NL4-3 Nef, they differ in their n-termini. However, they are closer matches to NL4-3.

While antibody behavior can be idiosyncratic, it remains best practice when possible to pair antibodies made from a given peptide epitope with matching sequences. For example, let’s consider some historical work in the Klotman lab. The antibody used in the following papers is alright:

Husain, Mohammad, Vivette D. D’Agati, John Cijiang He, Mary E. Klotman, and Paul E. Klotman. 2005. “HIV-1 Nef Induces Dedifferentiation of Podocytes in Vivo: A Characteristic Feature of HIVAN.” AIDS (London, England)19(April):1975–80.

Those used an epitope like HIV1 nef Antibody (2H12; 01-007) (MA1-71505, ThermoFisher). Per ThermoFisher, “This antibody reacts with HIV-1 Nef, B and C subtypes, BRU, IIIB, and HAN strains.” BRU (and HTLV-III) is for the most part the same as HXB2, and the 3' end of NL4-3 is HXB2.

docs.title: Check your genome references, carefully!
docs.text: Interestingly, the genome entry for HXB2, K03455.1 has a different nef/Nef sequence compared to pNL4-3 (see ). We sequenced verified NL4-3 constructs as plasmids and mouse transgenes (Gener et al. 2021), and we can confirm pNL4-3 nef/Nef is distinct from HXB2, despite historical evidence suggesting they should be identical. Goes to show that it remains important to not assume identity of key reagents!!!

docs.title: HIV drugs designed against reference strains, ignoring real world variability
docs.text: HIV drug discovery originally came about by trial and error. Recombinant proteins were made from early HIV clones. A search of “HIV-1” on July 15, 2021 in the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics Protein Databank (RCSB PDB) (Berman et al. 2000) returned 3646 structures. Per depositor-provided metadata, most HIV structure entries are from NY5 (n=81), HXB2 (n=125), BH10 (n=160), BRU (n=55), ARV2/SF2 (n=53), unspecified, or unspecified human immunodeficiency (n=56), human immunodeficiency virus 1 (1781). Most are HIV-1 M group B subclade/subgroup strains. NY5 is the 5’ half of NL4-3. While most HIV infections are with HIV-1 M B viruses, the availability of these limited structures has biased the implementation of rational design for the development of HIV therapeutics.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Problems and Challenges addressed by HIV Informatics
docs.text:
Chapter Abstract

Chapter 4 explicitly introduces the problems I addressed with HIV Informatics by my papers and/or meeting abstracts included in my dissertation.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Identifying AIDS as a clinical syndrome in 1981 was seminal. Identifying HIV as the cause of AIDS in 1983 was the next key event in the HIV/AIDS epidemic, now an established pandemic. A third key event was the completion of the first HIV-1 reference genome in 1985 (Ratner et al. 1985). This watershed event enabled screening and later diagnostic tests, molecular dissection of the virus, and improved drug development.

HIV/AIDS was not just an immunodeficiency. Many tissues could become infected by HIV, and patients presented heterogeneously. For example, elite controllers rarely got sick despite being demonstrably HIV-positive, or if they did, their immune decline took on a much more indolent course. As more HIV sequences were collected from patients, investigators began to better appreciate HIV sequence heterogeneity. This heterogeneity became apparent as viral evolution occurred in earlier treatment regimens with fewer, often more toxic, drugs were used prior to the advent of multi-drug regimens. Investigators began to try to model heterogeneous sequences within patients as quasispecies, focusing on clinically relevant segments of the pol gene: reverse transcriptase, protease, and later integrase. However, technological limitations prevented such HIV information from making it into patient diagnostics and monitoring until very recently. Instead, combination therapy was developed empirically, one clinical trial at a time. Today we rely on viral load as a clinical endpoint instead of capturing HIV sequence information directly. Exceptions are viral genotyping which is performed in resource-rich settings either before antiretroviral therapy initiation and/or in the event of a need for treatment interruption or reinitiation. Independently of HIV genotyping, molecular epidemiologists sequenced env genes to track the spread of HIV. All of this was done as new methods became available, and over many years. Since sequencing was not available earlier in the HIV/AIDS pandemic, HIV heterogeneity was never assessed as a contributing factor for differential progression of HIV. However, some evidence supports differences in infecting virus and differences in clinical outcome. For example, it is well known that patients infected with HIV-2, a distantly related virus believed to be caused by the entry of another primate immunodeficiency virus into the human population, usually causes a much less severe AIDS-like illness.

People living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) are living longer (Alejandro R Gener 2021), and to maintain this progress it remains important to determine which tissues can serve as reservoirs for HIV replication. Beyond preventing HIV replication, HIV treatment does not prevent HIV mRNA transcription or translation into HIV proteins (together: HIV gene expression). This is because in the context of viral suppression, HIV gene expression continues in these reservoir cells populations. It remains important to be able to recover HIV sequence information and to distinguish between HIV’s myriad nucleic acid forms (Gener and Kimata 2019) to be able to track HIV across the human body.

We now have the tools to address HIV heterogeneity in clinical samples. However, it serves to reason that it is beneficial to revisit defined key reagents before exploring HIV in heterogeneous clinical samples. HIV Informatics is a framework unifying HIV models, nucleic acid (re)sequencing, bioinformatics, and validation to maximize the HIV information gained from assays.

In Chapter 5 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021a), 6 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021b), 7 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021c), and 8 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021d) I revisited basic historical models of HIV-1 previously taken for granted with new methods. Reference reagents like HIV-1 plasmids or virus preparations (preps) are rarely routinely sequence (re)verified/(re)validated. That “re” is important to prevent a game of biological telephone from propagating into costly experimental error. Until recently, repetitive sequences in the 5’ and 3’ LTRs were ignored because of cost to validate them between in silico reference genomes and physical copies available through the AIDs Reagent Program (ARP; and more recently Addgene) or across individual labs. There is no standard annotation for HIV reference genomes. Annotation is a problem with HIV sequences. For example, the ones in Chapter 7 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021c) Table 1 lack gag-pol, and many complete HIV and HIV-related genomes lack feature annotations altogether. Many papers and textbooks fail to even include the gag-pol gene model, instead favoring out-of-date gag and pol as distinct. This may be a holdover from the study of endogenous retroviruses, or simple retroviruses1. That said, HIV is far from a simple retrovirus, and including molecular biologically relevant genes may facilitate better understanding.

docs.title: Validating HIV-1 reference genome(s)
docs.text: Chapter 5 dealt with comparing new nanopore long-read DNA sequencing to validate pHXB2_D, the only known physical copy of the canonical HIV-1 reference genome strain HXB2 (in silico as GenBank:K03455.1 and RefSeq:NC_001802.1) which is currently not available in the ARP. A recently rederived plasmid based on pNL4-3 backbone was included as a positive control. Variants were noted in pHXB2_D. This was surprising because physical key reagents like molecular clones are assumed to be identical to their in silico genome accessions. The repetitive elements in both plasmids’ HIV-1 LTRs were phased and validated with 1.) current gold-standard short-read (SR) 150 base-long Illumina sequencing and assembly and 2.) new long-read (LR) ~2000 base-long Nanopore DNA sequencing, assembly, and polishing. The bioinformatics applied depended on which methods were used. For example, SR aligners can usually only take SR data as input. An exception is Minimap2, which recently implemented SR alignment (Heng Li, personal communication). However, the internal algorithms used depend on data type. As such, aligners are often not interchangeable. Downstream analyses may be flexible. An exception is transcript modelers, which rely on accuracy of mapped reads to make transcript models and to perform transcript profiling. Transcript profiling estimates transcript abundance based on premade (user-provided) or de novo transcript models. De novo in this context means transcript models generated from a given sample only, without prior feature (gene or transcript) information. Variants were called manually based on K03455.1, and as such this was a resequencing experiment. LANL HIV Sequence Database’s HXB2 K03455.1 is modeled as a provirus with likely incorrectly phased long-terminal repeats (my first paper) (Gener et al. 2021). As this was the first time LR and SR data was used to evaluate an HXB2 sequence, this pHXB2_D assembly is currently the highest quality HXB2 assembly to-date.

docs.title: Redressing overly simplified HIV-1 mRNA models
docs.text:
Previously, HIV-1 mRNA was modeled roughly as 3 different classes of mRNAs: unspliced 9kb, singly spliced 4 kb, and doubly spliced ~2 kb mRNAs (Purcell and Martin 1993). The HIV research community took Purcell and Martin’s results and ran with them, focusing on the most common isoforms to design PCR primers for reverse transcription (RT) PCR with a gel band readout. This was subsequently adapted to real-time RT qPCR, which is currently a staple in many labs. The HIV research community also ran with the assumption that the first open reading frame (ORF) was the sole or predominant protein product in each isoform. Singly vs. doubly spliced classifications ignore the heterogeneity revealed by Schwartz et al., Purcell and Martin, and others. Newcomers Ocwieja et al. in 2012 and Nguyen Quang et al. in 2020 attempted to capture HIV splice junctions comprehensively but fell short of providing usable models and tractable bioinformatic pipelines which accommodate high-throughput and/or next-generation sequencing data. Their work has not yet been adopted widely, in part because their tables of splice junctions cannot be easily integrated into public database which accept formats like FASTA, GenBank, Gene transfer format (.gtf), etc.

HIV-1 review resources report discrepancies between earlier primary reports. For example, the ViralZone “HIV replication cycle” review says the following: “[HIV-1] mRNA transcripts are alternatively spliced into six mRNAs.” However, this review does not support this claim with specific citations, but I can deduce based on what I have seen so far in my readings. One isoform (#1) is unspliced HIV. That is believed to make Gag and Gag-pol. Another (#2) is gag-pol spliced out, yielding Vif. Another (#3) is gag-pol and vif spliced out, yielding Vpr. Another (#4) is gag-pol, vif, and vpr spliced out, yielding Vpu and Env. Another (#5) is gag-pol, vif, vpr, vpu, and env spliced out, yielding Tat and Rev. Last (#6), maximally spliced HIV can yield Nef only. Other reviews cite different numbers of isoforms (UCSF HIV InSite claims 30 (Schwartz et al. 1990)), and often stop short of linking isoforms with the open reading frames and therefore their HIV protein-coding capacity.

Chapter 6 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021b) defined models of HIV-1 mRNA explicitly, which had not been defined comprehensively before. My work in Chapter 6 offers others the chance to build their own models from their experiments if their data are of sufficient coverage and high quality (read length and read quality). My methods are backwards-compatible with SR RNA-seq. However, LR data is better for capturing splice junctions present in HIV-1 mRNA.

docs.title: A new HIV-1 virion model
docs.text:
Chapter 7 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021c) explored HIV virion mRNA directly as native RNA for the first time. While Nguyen Quang et al. in 2020 produced the highest-quality LR dataset from infected cell lysates, they were unable to produce HIV virion mRNA. We sequenced virion mRNA directly without cDNA sequencing and compared our results with the transcript models we built in Chapter 6 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021b). This was an important example of cross-validation using datasets from multiple labs and some open datasets. Lack of open datasets had limited progress in this space previously. My HIV virion mRNA results challenge the dogmatic assumption that HIV mRNA includes two full-length unspliced HIV mRNA transcripts of approximately 9.7 kb. I proposed the Hybrid Segmented Retrovirus model (Gener and Kimata 2020), of which HIV is the index example.

Chapter 8 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021d) revisited LR HIV mRNA datasets from Chapters 6 and 7 with LTR phasing from Chapter 5, with surprising results which challenge the current model of retroviral reverse transcription. Careful inspection of R variants across NL4-3 in Nguyen Quang et al. 2020’s and my native virion datasets show that LTRs do not homogenize as expected. This supports the model of HIV virion as a bag of heterogeneous HIV mRNAs as opposed to having two copies of full-length unspliced HIV mRNAs.

In Chapter 9 (Alejandro R. Gener 2021e) I built on lessons learned from implementing HIV Informatics in control systems as I attempt to maximize the information extracted from HIV-infected cadaveric brain tissue to clarify the contributions of different cell populations toward HIV gene expression during HIV encephalopathy.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Advancing HIV informatics in the DNA space
Chapter abstract
docs.text:
In Chapter 5, we sought to evaluate long- and short-read DNA-seq methods for recovering information from control HIV samples: 1.) a plasmid believed to contain the reference plasmid of HIV-1 HXB2, and 2.) a plasmid known to contain sequences based on NL4-3, the most common lab strain of HIV. The main text of this chapter is formatted as a manuscript in its current form that is in the process of being transferred for peer-review. It is available online as a preprint:

Gener, Alejandro R., Wei Zou, Brian T. Foley, Deborah P. Hyink, and Paul E. Klotman. 2021. “Reference Plasmid PHXB2_D Is an HIV-1 Molecular Clone That Exhibits Identical LTRs and a Single Integration Site Indicative of an HIV Provirus.” BioRxiv 611848.

In this work, I evaluated 2nd (Illumina) and 3rd generation (Oxford Nanopore) nucleic acid sequencing platforms to define the reference clone for HXB2, the reference strain of HIV-1. I validated the clone as a bona fide provirus, enabling its future use by investigators. In so doing, I was the first to cover an HIV provirus in its entirety in a single read, and first to unambiguously define a complete HIV haplotype with long-read DNA-seq (as opposed to quasispecies or partial gene model-based haplotypes from short-read DNA-seq).

Keywords: HIV-1, reagent verification, nanopore DNA sequencing, provirus, plasmid, sequence variability, resequencing, LTR phasing

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Sequence-verified molecular clones of HIV-1 reference HXB2 were thought lost. We sought to verify the identity of plasmid pHXB2_D, believed to contain a full-length copy of HIV-1 HXB2 model provirus, and a control plasmid pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP. We compared long- and short-read DNA sequencing, evaluating sample variability with resequencing (sequencing and mapping to reference) and de novo viral genome assembly. We obtained full-length HIV-1 and plasmid backbone with flanking host sequences supporting a single HXB2 integration event. We discovered 20 single nucleotide variants in pHXB2_D compared to reference HXB2, verified by short-read DNA sequencing. Contrary to the reference sequence, pHXB2_D had identical LTRs. No variants were detected in the HIV-1 segments of pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP, which retained distinct LTRs. Nanopore sequencing performed as expected, phasing LTRs, and covering full-length HIV. The discovery of variants in a reference plasmid demonstrates the need for sequence verification moving forward, in line with calls from funding agencies for reagent verification. These results illustrate the utility of long-read DNA sequencing to advance the study of HIV at single integration site resolution.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Much of what we know about human acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) came after isolating the causative agent, the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), and describing the viral genome information content. The HIV-1 isolate HXB2, also known as HTLV-III and HIV-1LAI or LAV/BRU (Barré-Sinoussi et al. 1983; Wain-Hobson et al. 1991), was the first full-length replication-competent HIV genome sequenced (Ratner et al. 1985). Derivative clones commonly called “HXB2” are still used for in vitro infection assays, including RNA (almost always cDNA (Gener and Kimata 2019)) sequencing (Figure 1A and Supplemental Table 1). Despite the availability of the HXB2 HIV-1 reference sequence (Ratner et al. 1985), no sequence is available for any complete and readily available HXB2 clone.

Figure 1: HIV information in pHXB2_D is recovered by long-read sequencing and mapping.

Figure 1A: HXB2 is still a commonly used resource. It is the reference HIV-1 genome, derived from one of the earliest clinical isolates. While older HIV samples are occasionally rediscovered, they are not made routinely available to researchers. All public HIV-1 RNA-seq datasets were obtained from the NCBI SRA with the following search phrase: “HIV-1” AND “RNA-seq”. Metadata from these 2527 runs (number current as of 7/21/2020) were used to make a pie chart summary.

Figure 1B: HIV sequence sources. HIV information comes from three main sources: proviruses (HIV sandwiched between two assumedly identical full-length long terminal repeats (LTRs)), unspliced HIV mRNAs (also known as viral genomes) starting from the transcription start site and ending in the 3’ LTR (Gener and Kimata 2019), and engineered proviruses recovered in their entirety or stitched together from multiple isolates like NL4-3 (Adachi et al. 1986).

Figure 1C: ONT library prep pipeline. Tagmentation cleaves double-stranded DNA, ligating barcoded PCR adapters (magenta). PCR-adapted DNA may be amplified. After amplification and cleanup, ONT sequencing adapters (green) are ligated. Barcoded samples may be pooled and sequenced.

Figure 1D: Newer basecallers increase read mean quality. Median (big dash) and quartiles (little dash). Effect of enzyme version was not statistically significant.

Figure 1E: Read stats with different callers/aligners. Median (big dash) and quartiles (little dash). Read lengths increase with higher fidelity Taq.

Figure 1F: Sequencing coverage with long- vs. short-read single-end 150 bp (trimmed to 142 bp) DNA sequencing. Long-read sequencing covers ambiguously mappable areas missed by short-read in HXB2 reference GenBank:K03455.1 (Supplemental Figures 3D,3E), but at the expense of accuracy near homopolymers longer than about 4 nucleobases (Supplemental Figure 5). Short-read mapping fails at repetitive elements longer than their read lengths (Supplemental Figures 3D,3E). Long read Minimap2 settings: map-ont -k15. Short read Minimap2 settings: Short reads without splicing (-k21 -w11 --sr -F800 -A2 -B8 -O12,32 -E2,1 -r50 -p.5 -N20 -f1000,5000 -n2 -m20 -s40 -g200 -2K50m --heap-sort=yes --secondary=no) (sr).

Table 1: Summary of pHXB2 sample divergence from reference HXB2.

Coverage numbers vary by input (albacore, guppy, FlipFlop basecalled FASTQ) and mapping method (Minimap2 vs. BWA-MEM). This information is provided as Supplemental Digital Content. Base-1 (first base is numbered 1, 2nd 2, etc.), relative to HXB2, Genbank:K03455.1. Changed base represented as upper-case. Annotated as codon if in protein-coding region. No deletions or insertions were predicted from manual inspection or supported by short-read sequencing. Abbreviations, ASP: antisense protein, RRE: rev-response element, NA: not applicable. Syn: synonymous mutation. Non: non-synonymous mutation. Stop: stop codon/non-sense mutation. LTR: long terminal repeat. RT: reverse transcriptase. IN: integrase. LANL: Los Alamos National Laboratory HIV Sequence Database. Data from three separate sequencing experiments on the same plasmid sample support these 20 sites. Note site 1-8 variants in 5’LTR have been previously reported (LANL), albethey ambiguously. These may also be incorrectly annotated as variants in nef.

HIV clones were originally made by digesting DNA from infected host cells with non-cutter restriction enzymes sparing HIV-1 sequence followed by ligation into an E. coli plasmid cloning vector (Figure 1B), allowing for low-error propagation (Shaw et al. 1984). Trace flanking host sequences were retained. These clones became available before tractable sequencing methods permitted routine sequence verification. As such, it was uncommon to sequence them. While funding agencies now require investigators to include in their proposals plans to validate their key reagents, these funders tend to leave the process up to investigators and may not always follow up on whether a given reagent is ever actually validated or revalidated between changes of hand. Investigators do not regularly validate their clones, in part because there is no universally accepted standard. Instead, a common practice is to assume a given clone, often kindly gifted from a colleague, is as reported. As such, we often do not truly know what we have been working with for 35+ years.

Making sense of the information from HIV sequencing experiments is complicated by many factors, including the cycling that all orterviruses (Krupovic et al. 2018) undergo between two major states (as infectious virion RNA and integrated proviral DNA Figure 1B), repetitive viral sequences like long terminal repeats (LTRs), non-integrated forms (Graf et al. 2011), rarity of integration events in vivo (reviewed in (Ito et al. 2017)), and alternative splicing of viral mRNAs (Cuesta et al. 2016). Short-read DNA sequencing provides some information, but analyses require high coverage and/or extensive effort (non-exhaustive examples (Bruner et al. 2019; Wymant et al. 2018)). These factors limit the ability to assign variants to specific loci within each provirus, as well as at the proviral integration site(s) (reviewed in (Pinzone and O’Doherty 2018)). Despite progress in the HIV DNA (Einkauf et al. 2019) and HIV RNA (Bonsall et al. 2018), (Banin et al. 2019), (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020), spaces, researchers have yet to observe the genome of HIV-1 as complete full-length provirus of integrated HIV DNA in a single read, hindering locus-specific studies. Complete here is defined from the beginning of the HIV 5’ LTR to the end of the 3’ LTR (Figure 1B). To this end, current long-read DNA sequencing clearly surpasses the limitations of read length of leading next-generation/short-read sequencing platforms. Here we used the MinION sequencer to sequence unknown HIV-1 plasmid pHXB2_D and a control known plasmid pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP in a pilot study focusing on coverage acquisition (as opposed to full-length sequencing), with the goal of evaluating the technology for future applications.

docs.title: HIV-1 plasmids
docs.text:
A plasmid, “pHXB2_D” (alternate names pHXB2, pHXB-2D), believed to contain the HIV-1 reference strain HXB2 (Fisher et al. 1985) was acquired from the NIH AIDS Reagent and Reference Program (ARP) via BioServe. pHXB2_D was believed to be a molecular clone (likely a restriction product of HXB2 proviral DNA inserted into an unknown cloning plasmid backbone) from one of the earliest clinical “HXB2” HIV-1 isolates. At the time of this work, it was unknown whether this plasmid was ever sequence-verified before or after the reference sequence for HXB2 was deposited.

The provenance of pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP, a reporter construct of pNL4-3 with a gag-pol deletion between base 1443 and 4553 is known. HIV-1 NL4-3 (pNL4-3) was a fusion of NY5 and LAV/HXB2 plasmids (Adachi et al. 1986) that to our knowledge are not readily available. pEVd1443 (Dickie et al. 1991) was a deletion construct made from pNL4-3 used to make several HIV-1 transgenic animals, including the FVB/N-Tg(HIV)26Aln/PkltJ (The Jackson Laboratory stock No: 022354) “Tg26” mouse. The deletion in pEVd1443 was made by SphI cutting between base 1443 and 1444 with binding site 1443-1448 and cutting at a BalI site at 4551-4556 with blunt cutting between 4553 and 4554. The EGFP cassette includes additional sequence upstream and downstream of EGFP coding sequence. SphI and BalI may still be used to excise EGFP cassette. A reporter construct was designed mimicking the pEVd1443 deletion: pNL4-3: ΔG/P-EGFP (Husain 2002). Dr. Wei Zou rederived pNL4-3: ΔG/P-EGFP at BCM (Li et al. 2018). Both constructs (plasmid and mouse) retained parts of gag and pol, with limited effects on protein-coding capacity, such as expression of p17 (Curreli et al. 2013). Bioinformatic resources do not regularly include non-ASCII characters such as “Δ”, occasionally converting these to the word “delta”. “Δ/delta” are historical abstractions away from wanting to convey a deletion relative to a sequence’s reference. Using Addgene naming conventions, we suggest pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP to replace the previous name pNL4-3: ΔG/P-EGFP for clarity.

docs.title: HIV-1 reference sequences
docs.text: The reference sequence of HXB2 is from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), Genbank accession number K03455.1. It runs from the beginning of the 5’ LTR to the end of the 3’ LTR, and is 9,719 bp. This is similar to another HIV-1 reference that NCBI uses, AF033819.3. This is a 9,181 base HXB2-like sequence that starts at the 97 bp repeat in the 5’LTR, continues with the 5’UTR (U5), extends past the 3’UTR (U3) to the end of the 97 bp repeat in 3’LTR, with one SNV at the vpu start codon aTg to aCg at position AF033819.3:560 or K03455.1:6063. The reference sequence of NL4-3 is as a plasmid with accession number AF324493.1. It runs from the beginning of the 5’ LTR to the end of the 3’ LTR, spanning 9,709 bp, and includes plasmid backbone with total length 14,825 bp.

docs.title: Long-read DNA sequencing
docs.text:
A plasmid containing HXB2 was sequence-verified with long-read nanopore sequencing on a MinION Mk1B (Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT), Oxford, United Kingdom). Unless otherwise noted, reagents and software were obtained from ONT. Briefly, stock plasmid was diluted to 5 ng final amount in ultrapure water (as two samples) and processed with Rapid PCR Barcoding kit SQK-RPB004 along with 10 other barcoded samples (not discussed further in this manuscript) following ONT protocol RPB_9059_V1_REVA_08MAR2018 (Figure 1C), https://store.nanoporetech.com/us/sample-prep/rapid-pcr-barcoding-kit.html. Two DNA polymerases were evaluated (barcode 10 used high-fidelity LA (for “long amplicon”) Taq (Takara); barcode 11 Taq (Sigma-Aldrich). Libraries were loaded onto a MinION flow cell version R9.4.1 and a 48-hour sequencing run was completed with MinKNOW (version 1.10.11). Residual reads from subsequent runs were pooled for final analyses. Long read data for pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP was generated in other barcoded experiments (not shown).

Raw data was basecalled (converted from FAST5 to FASTQ format) with Albacore version 2.3.4 (older basecaller), Guppy version 2.3.1 (current official at time of work), and FlipFlop (Guppy development config). Mapping to reference was done with Minimap2 (Li 2018) and BWA-MEM (Li and Durbin 2010), implemented in Galaxy (usegalaxy.org) (Afgan et al. 2016). Alignments (.bam and .bai files) were visualized in the Integrative Genomics Viewer (Robinson et al. 2011) unless otherwise noted. For de novo assembly, demultiplexed basecalled reads were fed into Canu version 1.8 (Walenz et al. 2017). Genome size was estimated to be 16 Kb from agarose gel of undigested, but naturally degraded linearized pHXB2_D (data not shown). SnapGene version 4.3.4 was used to manually annotate contigs from Canu. Blastn (NCBI) was used to identify unknown regions of pHXB2_D. Polishing was performed on ONT-only assemblies with Medaka (https://github.com/nanoporetech/medaka), in Galaxy. Medaka models: r941_min_fast_g303, r941_min_high_g303, r941_min_high_g330. Inference batch size (-b) = 100. The final pHXB2_D assembly and other full-length HIV clones from the ARP were aligned to the most recent human reference genome (hg38) with Minimap2 in Galaxy with the following parameters: Long assembly to reference mapping (-k19 -w19 -A1 -B19 -O39,81 -E3,1 -s200 -z200 --min-occ-floor=100).

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: Two-tailed Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare distributions in long-read data. P-values are reported over brackets delineating relevant comparisons. Calculations and graphing were done with GraphPad Prism for macOS version 8.0.2.

docs.title: Short-read DNA sequencing
docs.text: pHXB2_D and control pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP were provided as 35 ul at ~63 ng/ul to the Center for Computational & Integrative Biology DNA Core at Massachusetts General Hospital, an external DNA sequencing core specializing in high-throughput next generation (short-read) plasmid sequencing and assembly. Neither HXB2/pNL4-3 reference sequences nor pHXB2_D/pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP draft assemblies (from this work) were provided to core staff at the time of sequencing so that testing would remain masked. While the core’s exact library prep is proprietary, multiplexed library prep and 150 single-end ILMN sequencing were most likely performed on a MiSeq with platform-specific reagents (V2 chemistry, per their website) and barcoding. Data was returned as FASTQ. FASTQC (Andrews n.d.) was used in Galaxy for in-house data quality control, and read lengths were all 142 bp per this tool. Mapping as above.

docs.title: Sequence comparisons
docs.text: We used MAFFT v7.475 (Katoh, Rozewicki, and Yamada 2017; Katoh and Standley 2013) to compare the LTR sequences of pHXB2_D and HXB2, and pNL4-3 and pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP. For cladistics, we used BLAST at HIV-DB (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/BASIC_BLAST/basic_blast.html) to find other HXB2-like genomes. The top 50 BLAST hits included many sequences of pNL4-3 clones. pNL4-3 is an artificial recombinant of the NY5 clone with LAV and/or the HXB2 clone (Adachi et al. 1986). The recombination point is marked by an EcoRI restriction site. We then made a multi-sequence alignment with the final pHXB2_D assembly, the top BLAST hits, and the HIV-1 M group subtype reference set using GeneCutter (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/GENE_CUTTER/cutter.html), and built the maximum likelihood tree using IQ-tree (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/IQTREE/iqtree.html). pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP was not included in the above trees because of absence of divergence from pNL4-3 sequences outside of the EGFP cassette.

docs.title: Read length and LTR phasing
docs.text: Viewing mapped data from both pHXB2_D ONT experiments in IGV, the long reads had median read lengths >2000 bp, (Figure 1E) clearly covering each LTR (Figure 1F, Supplemental Figures 1, 3). This unambiguously enabled LTR phasing by physically linking each LTR to its respective location. Long reads <700 bp and short reads collapsed into one of either LTR (Figure 1F, Supplemental Figures 3D,3E). Mappers BWA-MEM and Minimap2 were chosen based on their ability to handle long and short reads. Other mappers were not evaluated. BWA-MEM mapped more ambiguously, piling partially mapped reads between each LTR; Minimap2 mapped with higher fidelity to reference without splitting reads. Coverage as sequencing depth was higher and more even from the higher fidelity LA Taq library (Supplemental Figure 1). pNL4-3 was believed to have distinct LTRs because it was a synthetic recombinant. The higher variant density in NL4-3 LTRs enabled mapping and phasing from short-read data only (Supplemental Figure 2).

docs.title: Single nucleotide variants (SNVs)
docs.text:
We counted 20 single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in this reference clone of HXB2 (Table 1, Supplemental Table 3, Supplemental Figure 3E). These mismatches were seen in all Canu assemblies (Supplemental Figures 4A,4B), verified in IGV and/or SnapGene, and were orthogonally verified by short-read sequencing performed by the external core given masked samples (Supplemental Figure 3E). These mismatches represent a ~0.21% divergence from reference HXB2 K03455.1 (20/9719), which was assumed to have perfect identity or 0% divergence. Transitions were more common (14/20) (Table 1), coinciding with a previous report of increased transitions over transversions in infection models, because transversions are more likely to be deleterious to viral replication (i.e.: to cause protein-coding changes) (Lyons and Lauring 2017). Indeed, almost half (9/20) of the observed SNVs occurred in protein-coding regions, even though 92% of HXB2 is coding (791/9719). Of those 9 SNVs in protein-coding regions, 4 caused non-synonymous mutations. One of those occurs in a region overlapping both gag and pol regions, however only pol exhibited a non-synonymous change from valine to isoleucine in p6, at base 2259 relative to HXB2. Other non-synonymous variants occurred at base 4609 (in p31 integrase, arginine to lysine), base 7823 (in ASP antisense protein, glycine to arginine), and base 9253 (in nef, isoleucine to valine). 11/20 SNVs were in LTRs (see Supplemental Figure 3 for counting based on mapping); 8/20 of these would have been missed with mapping-only variant calling or consensus. The longest HIV-mapping read (Figure 2) phased 16/20 SNVs (failed at sites 2,8,10,12, Table 1). pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP did not have HIV-1 or plasmid backbone variants supported by long and short reads outside of the EGFP cassette.

Figure 2: Longest read containing complete full-length HIV-1 reference HXB2.

The 5th longest read in the barcode 10 set (read ID 6fbf0205-5195-460e-8e28-930db50e5d79) contained full-length HIV-1. Query (full read) blastn against HIV (taxid:11676) returned 92.95% identity to HIV-1, complete genome (GenBank:AF033819.3). Limiting query to HXB2 (red) blastn against Nucleotide collection nr/nt returned 100% coverage and 93.02% identity to HIV-1 HXB2. This read was 11,487 bases long, with mean quality score 11.984396. Basecalled using Guppy 2.3.1 with FlipFlop config.

docs.title: Assembling HIV-1 plasmids
docs.text:
We assembled the previously undefined plasmid pHXB2_D (Supplemental Figures 4A,4B). Canu’s final output was a set of contiguous DNA sequences (contigs) as FASTA files. A consequence of assembling plasmid sequences with this tool was partial redundancy at contig ends (Supplemental Figure 4C). Manual end-trimming of contigs was performed in SnapGene based on an estimated length of 16 kb. Top blastn hits from barcode 10/LA Taq pHXB2 basecalled with FlipFlop were as follows: for the main backbone with origin of replication and antibiotic selection cassette for cloning, shuttle vector pTB101-CM DNA, complete sequence (based on pBR322), from 4352-8340; for the upstream element (relative to 5’ LTR), Homo sapiens chromosome 3 clone RP11-83E7 map 3p, complete sequence from 58,052 to 59,165; for the downstream element, cloning vector pNHG-CapNM from 10,204 to 11,666. Other identified elements included Enterobacteria phage SP6, complete sequence from 39,683 to 39,966. This was identified as the SP6 promoter, per SnapGene’s “Detect common features” feature. Identities of query to HXB2 and hits were all approximately 99%. The MGH CCIB DNA Core’s proprietary de novo UltraCycler v1.0 assembler (Brian Seed and Huajun Wang, unpublished) was able to assemble both 5’ and 3’ LTRs with short-read data only but may have collapsed SNVs into an artificial single consensus. Long-read mapping and assembly (and polished assemblies) orthogonally validated LTRs and supported a single HIV-1 HXB2_D haplotype (Supplemental Figure 4,6). A final LTR-phased and annotated assembly leveraging short and long reads is provided as pHXB2_D Genbank:MW079479 (embargoed until publication). Importantly, for pHXB2_D, each LTR was identical, which is distinct from the current HXB2 (K03455.1) (Figure 3A). Compared to pNL4-3_gag-pol(del1443-4553)_EGFP Genbank:MW928609 (embargoed until publication) , each LTR was distinct, but identical to pNL4-3’s distinct 5’ and 3’ LTRs (AF324493.1) (Figures 3B,6).
