docs.title: Transcript Modeling and Profiling (copied from HIV-1 NL4-3 mRNA Atlas)
docs.text: Data from Nguyen et al. 2020 was used to build HIV-1 transcript models (Gener 2021; Alejandro R. Gener et al. 2021). CD4+ T cells and/or PBMCs infected with VSVG-pseudotyped HIV-1 NL4-3 were sequenced with PCR-barcoded cDNA nanopore sequencing. Reads from CD4+ T cells were aligned with minimap2 -splice (Li 2018). Mapped reads as BAM were fed into StringTie (Kovaka et al. 2019; Pertea et al. 2015), default settings + long reads and -f 0.0001. StringTie was repeated with -merge and -f 0.0001 and -i. MSTRG1, MSTRG3, MSTRG4 were artifacts. MSTRG.2 was a high-confidence real set. The starting point was trimmed to 5’ R, and 3’ R was manually added due to likely technical drop off from mostly polyA reads. The final set of curated merged isoforms model the most frequent HIV-1 transcripts seen in CD4+ T cells and/or PBMCs infected by pseudotyped NL4-3. StringTie output before -merge includes transcript quantification. Merged models were used to perform transcript profiling by repeating StringTie with these new models.

docs.title: HIV-1 viruses
docs.text:
To generate infectious virus from plasmid clones of HIV-1 NL4-3, NLAD8, RHPA, and AD17, we transiently transfected 293T cells using ExtremeGENE 9 according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Roche). After 48hr, supernatants were collected from transfected cultures of cells, passed through 0.45μm-pore-size syringe filters, aliquoted, and saved at -80°C. The amount of infectious virus was determined by limiting dilution on TZMbl cells using a luciferase reporter assay as we have described (Misra et al. 2018).

Other HIV-1 strains used in this study were derived from infectious virus obtained from the NIH AIDS Reagent Program (89.6, SF162, 97USNG30, MN, ADA, 92UG038, 92UG029, ELI, JR-FL, and BaL). In short, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from leukopacks of anonymous blood donors purchased from the Gulf Coast Blood Center (Houston, TX) using Lymphocyte Separation Medium (Sigma-Aldrich). Cultures of PBMCs were stimulated with phytohemagglutinin PHA-P and IL-2 (50U/ml) in RPMI1640 complete (supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 2mM L-glutamine, and 100U/ml penicillin/ 100μg/ml streptomycin) for 2 days prior to inoculation with HIV-1. After infection, PBMCs were cultured for an additional 10-15 days in RPMI complete with 50U/ml IL-2. Virus production was confirmed by testing supernatants for HIV-1 p24 by ELISA (Advanced Bioscience Laboratories). Supernatants were collected from infected cultures of PBMCs, passed through 0.45μm-pore-size syringe filters, aliquoted and saved at -80°C. The amount of infectious virus was determined by limiting dilution titration of the virus stocks on PHA-stimulated PBMCs and assay for infectious virus production after 10-14 days of infection by HIV-1 p24 ELISA.

HIV-SX was generously provided by M.R. Ferguson and W.A. O’Brien (“SX”) of the University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, TX.

docs.title: Viral RNA isolation
docs.text: RNA was extracted using the MagMAX-96 viral RNA isolation kit (Applied Biosystems) with a Kingfisher Flex Purification System (ThermoFisher) described by the manufacturer with the following modifications: 200μl of viral lysate was added to 200μl of freshly prepared Lysis/Binding Solution and allowed to incubate for at least 15min (no more than 1hr). Samples were loaded into 96-well deep well Kingfisher plates and processed following kit instructions. Each sample was eluted into 50ul of Elution Buffer in duplicate into individual DNA LoBind 1.5ml microcentrifuge tubes (Eppendorf) for storage at -80°C until use in sequencing.

docs.title: Long-read native RNA sequencing
docs.text:
Extracted RNA was sequenced across three MinION Mk1B sequencers (Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT), Oxford, UK) (Figure 1A). Briefly, 9ul of extracted viral RNA eluate was carried over and processed with Direct RNA kit SQK-RNA002 following ONT protocol DRS_9080_v2_revF_22Nov2018, Last updated: 19/07/2019. This protocol recommended 1 round of cDNA "first-strand” synthesis for the purpose of breaking up RNA 2º structure, however these cDNA strands are ultimately not sequenced. The reverse transcriptase kit used: SuperScript IV First Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen). The ligase used: T4 DNA ligase (NEB). Libraries (except for NL4-3) were loaded onto one of 5 MinION RevD flow cells, pore R9.4.1. and sequencing runs approximating 6 to 11 hours were completed with MinKNOW (v3.5.5). The pilot NL4-3 used a R9.4 RevC flow cell. Runs were stopped manually in MinKNOW based on empirical assessment of HIV-1 sequence coverage while Live Basecalling (ONT) was enabled. Between runs, flow cells were washed with Flow Cell Wash Kit (EXP-WSH003) (Version: WFC_9088_v1_revB_18Sep2019). Flow cells exhibiting increasing failed reads, or abrupt changes in membrane potential (bottoming out at -250mV) were replaced with new flow cells. Flow cell resting potential was set at -180mV at the beginning of each run, and MinKNOW was used to adjust voltage automatically at mux scans every 30min during the runs.

Figure 1A: Native sequencing of HIV-1 virion mRNA.

Figure 1A: Native RNA sequencing of HIV-1. Native RNA (also called direct RNA sequencing (DRS)) library protocol. To decrease sample variability, neutralized HIV from the supernatant of in vitro infected cells was processed with MagMAX-96 viral RNA isolation kit (Applied Biosystems) on a Kingfisher Flex Purification System (ThermoFisher). The reverse transcription (RT) step increases sequencing throughput. RT is believed to stabilize RNA. Method figure adapted from Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK (http://nanoporetech.com/). Salmon denotes forward-oriented reads in all subsequent figures. US = unspliced.

Raw data was basecalled from FAST5 to FASTQ with Guppy high-accuracy model v3.3.0. Passed and failed reads from live basecalling were collapsed with skipped reads (FAST5 which were not basecalled by the end of sequencing runs) into per-sample datasets for this study based on the observation that HIV-mapping reads could be recovered from failed read folders. SAMTOOLS stat and flagstat (Wysoker et al. 2009) were used for mapping stats from BAM files from minimap2 (Li 2018) implemented in Galaxy (Afgan et al. 2016) (usegalaxy.eu or usegalaxy.org). HIV-mapped basecalled reads were fed into Canu v2.1.1 (Walenz et al. 2017), with genomeSize=9k. Contigs from NLAD8 were polished with medaka (Ltd. 2020) with model r941_min_high_g330. SnapGene v5.0.4 was used to manually annotate contigs from Canu. Contigs were interrogated with multisequence alignments (MSAs) with MAFFT (Katoh, Rozewicki, and Yamada 2017) and visualized with Archaeopteryx 0.9921 beta (170712) (NEW FIGURE). To verify detected HIV-1 splice isoforms, sample-specific transcript models (as .gtf) were made with StringTie (Kovaka et al. 2019; Pertea et al. 2015), and compared to those seen in the following long-read HIV-1 datasets. Generalized transcript models were made by mapping idealized 89.6 (Karen E. Ocwieja et al. 2012) or NL4-3 (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020) reads to available references (Table 1).

docs.title: HIV-1 reference genome sequences
docs.text:
The general reference sequence of HIV-1 used in Figure 2 was from NCBI, accession number Genbank:AF033819.3. This is a 9,181 base HXB2-like sequence that starts at the 96 bp repeat in the 5’LTR, continues with the 5’UTR (U5), extends past the 3’UTR (U3) to the end of the 96 bp repeat in 3’LTR, with one SNV at the vpu start codon aTg to aCg at position AF033819.3:560 or K03455.1:6063 (Alejandro R Gener et al. 2021). Sample-specific references were used when available (Table 1).

Figure 2: Native HIV-1 virion mRNAs mapped to general reference AF033819.3 and sample-specific references.

With splice-aware minimap2, differentially spliced introns and exons become evident. Spliced HIV-1-mapping reads occurred at higher frequency than individual host transcripts (not shown; Supplemental Table 1). Reads are colored based on orientation relative to reference. Salmon: forward. Lavender: reverse. All HIV-mapping reads observed occurred in the forward orientation. HIV genome modeled near the transcription start site (TSS) to end of the repeat in the 3’LTR. The packaging element ψ occurs downstream of the TSS, between the end of the 5’LTR and beginning of gag. Most recovered HIV-1 reads lacked the packaging (ψ) element. This may have been due to degraded RNA and/or breaks in the DNA-RNA heteroduplex, RNA secondary structure. Compare to Figure 4. Portions of NLAD8, HIV1-SX, and NL4-3 partially matched AF324493.2 (absence of green (A)/blue (C)/yellow (G)/red (T/U)) stipes in reads) (Supplement).

For NLAD8, Full-length coverage (9,166/9,181~99.8%) achieved. Visualized in Integrative Genomics Viewer . Coverage over env sufficient for cladistics (Figure 5). Top left: general mapping. Top right, bottom row: Strain-specific reference mapping. Top right: pNL4-3. Bottom left: AD8. Bottom right: in silico NLAD8 based on information from AIDS Reagent Program. NLAD8 complete genome was not available from NCBI. Gray in coverage plot indicates per-base consensus accuracy ≥ 80%. Note that NLAD8 is a chimera between NL4-3 (all minus portion of env) and AD8 (portion of env) (used as a reference here). The reference sequence for NL4-3 is a complete plasmid sequence, pNL4-3. Note the difference in scales. Visualized in Integrative Genomics Viewer .

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: After basecalling, read lengths and mean quality scores are reported by MinKNOW. Graphing was done with GraphPad Prism 8 for macOS v8.3.0. As samples were not compared directly to each other, additional statistics were not calculated.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
HIV-1-mapping reads were recovered in all (n=15) experiments (Figure 1, Figure 2). Three out of 15 strains had full coverage, defined as read length spanning from the canonical TSS (5’ R repeat) to the 3’ R repeat and mapped to AF033819.3. These were: 89.6 (9,166/9,181~99.8%), AD17 (9,164/9,181~99.8%), and NLAD8 (9,166/9,181~99.8%). Seven out of 15 strains had majority coverage, defined as > 50% relative to AF033819.3. These were: 97USNG30 (6,992/9,181~76.2%), BaL (8,597/9,181~93.6%), ELI (6,987/9,181~76.1%), MN (5,995/9,181~65.3%), NL4-3 (4,715/9,181~51.4%), RHPA (4,745/9,181~51.7%), and HIV1-SX (5,561/9,181~60.6%). Three out of 15 strains had moderate coverage <50% and >25% relative to AF033819.3. These were: 92UG038 (3,678/9,181~40.1%), JR-FL (2,814/9,181~30.7%), and SF162 (2,601/9,181~28.3%). Two out of 15 strains had lower coverage <25% relative to AF033819.3. These were: 92UG029 (2,007/9,181~21.9%), and ADA (1,981/9,181~21.6%).

Figure 1B: Read lengths for HIV-1-mapping reads sequenced in this study.

Figure 1B: Read lengths for HIV-1-mapping reads sequenced in this study. Violin plot of read length. Log2-scaled. Median (big dash) and quartiles (little dash). All native RNA reads are longer than most short DNA-seq reads. Note: Reads from multiple runs either live-basecalled or skipped reads basecalled afterward were concatenated. For Figures 1B and 1C: after basecalling, read length and mean quality score are reported in a sequencing_symmary.txt file in MinKNOW. For skipped reads (reads not basecalled by timed or forced end of sequencing runs), basecalling in standalone Guppy provides the same sequencing_symmary.txt information. For HIV-1-mapping reads, this information is provided in Figure 1. To pull this information, unique read IDs aligning to Genbank:AF033819.3 (with minimap2) were concatenated into a master list and used as follows (with example file names): egrep -f MASTERLIST.txt sequencing_symmary.txt > HIV-mapping_sequencing_symmary.txt. Data was wrangled in Microsoft Excel for Mac version 16.29.1.

Figure 1C: Read mean quality scores for HIV-1-mapping reads sequenced in this study.

Figure 1C: Read mean quality scores for HIV-1-mapping reads sequenced in this study. Violin plot of mean quality score. Median (big dash) and quartiles (little dash). Note: Reads from multiple runs either live-basecalled or skipped reads basecalled afterward were concatenated.

In general, higher titer (TCID50/ml) samples (Table 1) were more likely to produce more and longer reads. To maximize the number of processed samples, flow cells were reused until exhausted. As such, an exact comparison between titer and throughput was not appropriate. Reads mapped well regardless of whether HXB2-like or sample-specific references were used (Figure 1D, Figure 2, Supplemental Table 1). We deferred analysis of sparce human-mapping RNA.

docs.title: Apparent transcription start site (TSS), and alternative TSS
docs.text:
For samples with 5’ R-spanning reads, apparent TSS were evaluated (Figure 5). 20/33 reads support most common TSS_NLAD8 is GGTT|AGACC 454+12=466^454+13=467 (HXB2/89.6 coordinates), with “A” being the first base. For 89.6, 2/3 reads support most common TSS_89.6 is GGTT|AGACC 454+12=466^454+13=467 (HXB2/89.6 coordinates), with “A” being the first base. 7/11 reads support most common TSS_AD17 is GGTT|AGACC 454+12=466^454+13=467 (HXB2/89.6 coordinates), with “A” being the first base. 2/3 reads support most common TSS_ELI is GGTT|AGACC 454+12=466^454+13=467 (HXB2/89.6 coordinates), with “A” being the first base. For SX, 1/1 read support TSS_SX is GGT|TAGACC 454+11=465^454+12=466 (HXB2/89.6 coordinates), with “T” being the first base. For NL4-3, 1/1 read support TSS_NL4-3 is GGTT|AGACC 454+12=466^454+13=467 (HXB2/89.6 coordinates), with “A” being the first base.

Figure 5: Ambiguity at 5’ end of native mRNA reads.

Top: HIV-1 apparent TSS most often occurs at the 14th base in the 5’ R repeat. However, this is likely not the true start of the transcript. We present these results to make viral sequencing community members aware of this native (direct) RNA sequencing artifact. Note uracil (U) in mRNA is converted arbitrarily to thymidine (T) in most references. This convention was maintained in this figure.

Middle: control ENO2 RNA appears to be able to cover 5’. However, this is not the start of the transcript. Assemblies ~22 bp upstream of the above “ATG” were recovered by assembling the NLAD8 basecalled reads with canu and genome size set to 1.4k (not shown). It remains unknown how long the control templates (ENO2 mRNA that was sequenced) actually were.

Bottom: cDNA with most reads starting at beginning of R. Some reads lacked portions of TAR.

We compared our TSS results above to the only other relevant work, which included cDNA ONT sequencing of NL4-3-infected primary CD4+ T cells(Nguyen Quang et al. 2020). Most HIV-mapping cDNA reads started at the beginning of the R repeat. Our uncorrected transcript models based on Nguyen et al.’s cDNA datasets supported actual TSS occurring before R, with small leader sequence “GTACT” upstream of the R’s G triplet. However, the read data supports actual TSS at the first G in R’s G triplet (Figure 5).

There was a class of reads which started downstream of R start. These occurred with both forward and reverse cDNA strands, suggesting that these were not an artifact of reverse-transcription during library preparation.

Another class of reads was noted, corresponding to early terminating gag-spanning reads which seemed to stall before reaching pol. These started at the HIV main TSS noted above and occurred independently of polyA sequences or alternative polyA signals (AATAAA; see below). Another potential stall point occurred in the middle of vpu, however this site was “A” rich, and may have been selected by polyA library prep. A second TSS seemed to occur downstream of gag ORF, around position 850-1130 relative to AF324493.2. It is not spliced with other HIV-1 segments, and the significance of this feature remains unknown.

docs.title: Antisense protein and/or Antisense mRNA
docs.text: While coverage over HIV-1 was sufficient to recover sense HIV-1 in all 15 samples, we did not recover any antisense HIV-1 transcripts in virion-associated mRNA (Figure 2, Supplemental Table 1).

docs.title: 3’ bias
docs.text:
All experiments demonstrated strong 3’ coverage bias over HIV-1 (Figure 2). This was also seen in control ENO2 mRNA (Supplemental Figure 1). Recovered read lengths from the control template exhibited consistent decay. Evaluating the reduction in coverage across samples at positions 1,200 and 200 yielded an average loss of 65.55% (SD = 10.71.%) of recovered transcripts per 1kb. (Supplemental Table 2). Furthermore, when we removed the outlier NL4-3 sequencing run from the analysis, which was completed with previously used but still functional R9.4 RevC flow cells and RNA002, the average loss was 68.41% (SD = 0.9685%).

The coverage profile of HIV-mapping reads from native RNA data exhibited a decrescendo pattern, with coverage diminishing as one advanced further from the main 3’ LTR. This was different than the patterns seen in NL4-3 cDNA ONT(Nguyen Quang et al. 2020) (Figure 4: cDNA ONT vs. native ONT ). In that study, it was clear that several internal polyA sites were activated. These represent a potential new source of HIV transcripts.

Figure 4: cDNA ONT vs. native ONT.

The saw-toothed pattern observed in cDNA PCR-barcoded ONT cannot be fully explained by ONT RT adapter ligation (polyA selection), nor are peaks otherwise coincident with incidental polyA-rich sequences. Data from Nguyen et al. 2020 from HIV-1 CD4+ T cells from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Mapped to pNL4-3. Blue arrows point to stark changes in coverage coincident with polyA signals (annotations tracks below Reference Annotations in red). The yellow arrow is the canonical HIV-1 NL4-3 polyA signal. Note both forward and reverse oriented reads from double-stranded cDNA amplicons. This pattern was consistent across replicates. The consequence of premature polyadenylation may be truncated pol with activated protease. Compare to Figure 2, where 15 HIV-1s exhibit a single “tooth”, or coverage peak at 3’ polyA site followed by decay. PolyA motifs: https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/28/1/127/219620.

docs.title: Splicing vs. ONT artifacts vs. other biological phenomena
docs.text:
We observed reads with large deletions relative to reverence AF033819.3 in higher coverage experiments using default ONT minimap2 settings (e.g., NLAD8 in Figures 2M). These deletions occurred near splice sites (Sertznig et al. 2018) found in other HIV-1 strains (Bruner et al. 2017; Hiener et al. 2017; Ho et al. 2013; Lee et al. 2017; Pollack et al. 2017; Simonetti et al. 2021), including 89.6(Karen E. Ocwieja et al. 2012). We reanalyzed our datasets with splice-aware settings and observed HIV splice isoforms in 10 out of 15 virion samples (Figure 2). Of the samples with full-length HIV viral genomes recovered, spliced reads were observed in 89.6 0.7% (1 out of 139; numerators based on generic or specific reference mapping in Supplemental Table 1), AD17 1.7% (16/633), and NLAD8 7.5% (77/1021). Spliced reads were also observed in 97USNG30 0.9% (2/225), BaL 0.6% (3/479), ELI 2.4,% (4/150), MN 3.7% (2/54), NL4-3 6.3% (3/48), RHPA 4.2% (1/24), and SX 1.6% (4/247) when mapped to their respective references or AF033819.3. RHPA’s isoform and one from AD17 are interesting ones which support the stability of a gag and gag-pol product spliced to downstream elements, respectively. Some false positives were seen when BaL reads were mapped to another HIV reference, pNL4-3 (Gener and Kimata 2020). These reads partially mapped to pNL4-3 5’LTR while also mapping to its 3’LTR (distinct from a supplementary alignment) and are minimap2 artifacts of read errors in LTRs, in contrast to true positives which also exhibited conserved smaller exons (Sertznig et al. 2018). Besides lacking ψ (psi) packaging element (necessary), 3’LTR (necessary), and RRE (sufficient), false positives are likely too short to be packaged (e.g., very few randomly distributed small human mRNAs were recovered (Supplemental Table 1). Other experiments either did not have as many transcriptional features or lacked coverage sufficient to observe splicing.

We compared our sequencing coverage profiles with those from Ocwieja et al. and Nguyen et al. While ours exhibited a decrescendo pattern (from higher coverage to lower coverage) as one progressed further from the adaptor ligation point, Nguyen et al.’s exhibited a saw-toothed pattern (Figure 4: cDNA ONT vs. native ONT).

docs.title: Bespoke vs. general transcript models
docs.text: To date, the best long-read sequencing dataset had been the NL4-3 cDNA PCR-barcoded experiments by Nguyen et alia from 2020. However, HIV splicing studies rarely if ever include explicit transcript models, limiting the studies’ utility. Thankfully, new tools such as StringTie (Kovaka et al. 2019; Pertea et al. 2015) can model transcription directly from long reads. We constructed transcript models using empirically determined StringTie settings, cross-validated by inspecting mapped reads in IGV. The resulting bespoke NL4-3 transcript model represents a “plug-and-play” transcript model set as .gtf file that is appropriate for use to aid in mRNA detection and quantification all NL4-3 RNA-seq experiments. Ocwieja et al. in 2012 used competing long-read DNA sequencing technology (PacBio) to provide a high-quality long cDNA amplicon dataset from total mRNA from lysed HIV-1 89.6-infected cells (Karen E. Ocwieja et al. 2012). While coverage in our present study was insufficient to model most transcripts directly, the robustness of long-read mapping as seen above in our results supported the use of the PacBio HIV-1 89.6 dataset for use as an approximate template to make generalizable HIV-1 transcript models. We mapped Ocwieja et al.’s data onto general and specific HIV-1 references used in our study. We considered our deepest dataset: NLAD8. NLAD8’s transcription start site (TSS) was at position ~468; transcription end site (TES) ~9,628 (coverage at least 10). NLAD8 mRNA length was therefore 9,628-468=9,160, which is approximate to AF033819.3’s length of 9,181. We adapted transcript models made with these start and end coordinates. These actual (NL4-3) and approximate hybrid HIV-1 transcript models support all the native spliced reads reported here. We present these new models as plug-and-play HIV-1 transcript models for future HIV-1 work in the time that deeper complete reference-specific HIV-1 transcript models and validated transcript sets are made.

docs.title: Putative SNV calls
docs.text: Samples with available reference genomes as GenBank accessions were manually evaluated for putative SNVs (pSNVs), including small insertions and deletions, under the conditions: 1) that there were at least 10 reads at a given locus; and 2) that the reference allele occurred less than or equal to 50% of the time. See Supplemental Table 3 for a list of pSNVs directly called from native RNA-seq. Combined, the average (putative) total mutation rate (excluding SX) was 0.008684598, 0.8684598% (SD = 0.007424836). The average (putative) non-redundant mutation rate (excluding SX) was 0.004649196, 0.4649196% (SD = 0.004564091). Supplemental Figures 2, 5-7 include pSNVs, small insertions, deletions. Polishing reduced the amount of pSNVs near homopolymers and dimer runs. A small deletion was observed in a region of NLAD8 outside of env (Supplemental Figure 2). This small deletion was apparent when mapped to AD8 AF004394.1, but absent in pNL4-3 AF324493.2, and had a different coverage profile compared to homopolymer runs (Supplemental Figure 3). Nguyen et al. 2020’s CD4+ T cell ONT cDNA data did not have clear pSNVs outside of ONT problem areas.

docs.title: Comparative transcriptomics
docs.text:
HIV-1-mapped (AF033819.3) reads from 89.6, 97USNG30, AD17, BaL, ELI, HIV1-SX, MN, and NLAD8 (Supplemental Figures 9 and 10) were assembled into contigs with Canu, a leading de novo long read genome assembler (Walenz et al. 2017). For sequences with GenBank accessions with complete genomes, the contigs’ phylogenetic tree resembled their references’ by maintaining tight clustering (Figure 6). Even with sub-genomic contigs, general relationships (such as similarity to NL4-3 in the cases of NLAD8 and HIV-SX) were maintained. By mapping reads to references we observed that phasing (the ability to tie variants to individual viral genome equivalents (also called chromosomes and/or haplotypes) was possible with native RNA reads (Supplemental Figure 7). We wanted to test whether this could be leveraged to study viral transcript heterogeneity directly. All FASTQ were converted to FASTA, concatenated, made into a MSAs, and visualized as a tree (Figure 6). Surprisingly, sample relationships were maintained despite per-read noise. Note neither contigs nor reads were polished.

Figure 6: ONT native RNA + Canu de novo assembly sufficient for comparative transcriptomics.

docs.title: First complete full-length sequences from infectious HIV-1 strains
docs.text: In this study we were able to completely (Ladner et al. 2014) sequence the genomes of three HIV-1 strains from virion-associated RNA (Figure 1 and 2). Here, we defined complete or full-coverage of full-length HIV-1 viral RNA as the region capable of sustaining viral replication with reverse transcription and integrase activity (Hu and Hughes 2012). This corresponds to the region from the 5’LTR-mediated transcriptional start site (TSS) and the repeat region after the end of 3’ U3. These dimensions are different than the dimensions of HIV-1 provirus (Gener 2019). To our knowledge, this is the first time the HIV-1 virus has been natively sequenced from the TSS to end of 3’LTR. As reported for HIV-1 in a DNA context (Gener 2019), ONT surpassed the read length limitations of short read RNA-seq. Data were sufficient for putative SNV detection over regions with coverage ≥10 reads, as well as direct de novo assembly from native RNA reads, with a maximal assembly length of 97% from strain NLAD8.

docs.title: Mapping
docs.text: High sequence variability across HIV isolates between and within patients and historically lower per-read accuracy represent two hypothetical challenges to detecting native HIV reads. Interestingly, newer long-read mappers such as minimap2 were robust to references used (Mapping quality >50). We saw slightly more recovered reads when we mapped our reads to sample-specific references with greater homology (Figures 2A, 2B, 2G, 2H, 2K, 2L, 2M, and 2N (these were moved to supplement)). These observations enabled informed use of others’ public long-read HIV-1 data to create tentative reference-anchored HIV-1 transcript models in the time that bespoke long-read transcript data is generated for each reference strain or clinical isolate.

docs.title: Apparent transcription start site (TSS)
docs.text: The HIV-1 TSS is one of the most well-studied/characterized viral RNA structures. Many have assumed that the TSS includes full-length R repeat sequence. This was not the case in any of the sequences with 5’ coverage. Our observations support the first base of HIV-1 being the 14th nucleotide of the 5’ R repeat, starting with the “A” in U11-U12 | A13-G14. This may have been obscured in the past because TSS occurs in the R repeats, 96 bp repeats within the larger ~654 bp LTR repeat. 5’ capping in the context of mRNA was reported to be problematic for ONT (Parker et al. 2020). On closer inspection, there was no left clipping in the 5’-spanning HIV-1 reads (NEW FIGURE). Full-length control ENO2 RNA reads were recovered when mapped to coding ENO2. However, that mapping strategy did not include ENO2’s 5’ UTR. We took basecalled reads from NLAD8 and assembled with canu and genome size 1.4k. We recovered multiple samples approximately 22 bp upstream of the ENO2 “ATG”. Another group had already performed the ideal experiments to identify the TSS (s) HIV-1 mRNA, albeit from cell lysate. They used cDNA sequencing, followed by PCR barcoding to minimize PCR bias, and their HIV transcripts map the full span of HIV-1, with slight variability. We conclude that virion-associated/packaged mRNA is still best modeled from the beginning of the R repeat, and community members should be aware of the difference between apparent and actual TSS between ONT’s native RNA (direct RNA) and cDNA sequencing.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text: These experiments represent a proof-of-concept demonstrating ONT’s ability to cover HIV mRNA completely (Figures 2A, 2E, and 2M (moved to supplement)), roughly dependent on the titer of viruses used for library prep (Table 1). The amount of starting material used (by TCID) across these 23 sequencing runs as 15 experiments is approximately consistent (within an order of magnitude) with viral loads of 500-1,000 copies/mL (Marozsan et al. 2004). Neither cDNA ONT nor cDNA PCR ONT libraries were evaluated in the present study. Coverage as total number of bases sequenced divided by reference length was not informative due to strong 3’ bias and target length of complete HIV-1 viral mRNA.

docs.title: 3’ bias
docs.text:
We were able to recover full-length HIV RNA reads from three samples. This was in part due to strong 3’ bias inherent to the RNA002 library. The first adapter used by the RNA002 kit, RTA, selects for polyA (Workman et al. 2018) (Figure 1A). There was relatively consistent coverage loss presenting as a decrescendo pattern (with coverage decreasing distal from RTA ligation point), except near areas of known complex 2º RNA structure (Anon n.d.). The first strand cDNA step is supposed to ameliorate 2º RNA, but these might not be completely abrogated—for example, the region around the rev response element in higher-coverage experiments exhibited slight changes in average loss of recovered transcripts per 1,000 bases (Figure 2). However, a useful consequence of the 3’ bias is easier phasing between 5’ and 3’LTR regions, which is difficult or impossible to tell apart using classic RNA-seq (short-read DNA-seq (Gener 2019)) (Supplemental Figure 12). There were no reads spanning full-length 5’LTR in any of our native RNA experiments; these occurred in HIV PCR + DNA ONT experiments (Gener 2019).

Included in the RNA002 library kit is control RNA. By determining the percent loss per 1kb, at least 2,500x coverage over the 3’LTR may be necessary to guarantee observation of full-length unspliced HIV reads (~9kb) at a depth sufficient to call SNVs at the 5’ end of transcripts (with the recommended ~60x coverage for Canu). At current sequencing throughput, this is equivalent to about one MinION RevD flow cell, with possibly multiple technical replicates of individual libraries. Higher-titer virus stocks were associated with higher coverage, although the sequencing time was not held constant.

docs.title: Splicing
docs.text:
NLAD8 (Figure 2M) had high enough coverage toward the middle of HIV to easily see deletions in reads relative to reference. Without prior information, these read deletions might be artifacts from library prep (with T4 DNA ligase), or from transcription of previously observed HIV-1 deletion-prone proviruses (Bruner et al. 2017; Hiener et al. 2017; Ho et al. 2013; Lee et al. 2017; Pollack et al. 2017), or splicing. Evidence supporting splicing includes our observations of splicing events from analyzing a short-read virion (cDNA) RNA-seq experiment (collected by Siarhei Kharytonchyk and submitted by Matthew Eckwahl) (Supplemental Figure 12). This incompletely published experiment most likely used pNL4-3, a commonly used synthetic lab-adapted clone of HIV-1. Another group used competing long-read technology (PacBio) to provide a high-quality long PCR dataset from HIV cDNA on HIV-1 89.6 (Karen E. Ocwieja et al. 2012), but they did not enrich for virion. Instead, they isolated total mRNA from lysed infected cells. Mapping peaks in our data occurred at sites of known exons. On closer inspection, these reads exhibited clipping indicating their being part of a spliced read. Selecting the “splicing”-aware option in minimap2 instead of the default ONT option allowed us to see many more spliced mRNAs (Figure 2). Finding so many spliced HIV mRNAs in samples enriched for virions supported our hypothesis that spliced viral mRNAs are normally packaged into HIV virion, with interesting implications for HIV pathogenesis. This is in line with previous observations by others (Bruner et al. 2017; Hiener et al. 2017; Ho et al. 2013; Lee et al. 2017; Pollack et al. 2017; Simonetti et al. 2021) who noted integration of replication-deficient HIV sequences (including sequences with large gaps). Our work fundamentally changes our understanding of how HIV might introduce information into cells, augmenting HIV’s ability to cause cytopathic effects after infection. A new model of HIV virion mRNA would represent a shift in the understanding of the HIV genome, from a ~9kb integrating retrovirus to a ~9kb + splice variant hybrid segmented retrovirus (Figure 7). Acknowledging this shift would improve detection of retroviral sequences so that we may follow the virus better as newer tools become available.

Figure 7B: Model: HIV virion contents fall along a spectrum, with consequences for resultant integrants.

We observed that HIV-1 virions had a range of packaged splice isoforms (Supplemental Table 1).

docs.title: pSNV calls from ONT Native RNA
docs.text:
Strain-specific reference mapping was performed on 89.6, 92UG029, BaL, ELI, MN, NL4-3, and NLAD8 (Figure 3 (moved to supplement)). Abundance of coverage allowed us to evaluate pSNVs, as well as small insertions and deletions, in areas with ≥ 10x coverage (minimum recommended by Canu documentation). The average mutation rate across sequenced samples (Supplemental Table 3) was estimated to be 0.00698528. This meant that for each full-length HIV-1 virion (say with respect to the HIV-1 reference AF033819.3) one would expect 0.00698528 x 9,181bases= ~64 pSNVs, possibly contributing to altered protein products (Gener 2019). We introduce Context Dependency Variant Classification (Supplemental Information) as new nomenclature to emphasize that variants occurring in information-dense regions can have complex context-dependent effects.

Figure 3: Summary of recovered reads.

Colors are arbitrary and for contrast. Using splice-aware mapping and/or mapping to a more specific HIV-1 reference (when available) led to a slight increase in recovered reads. 92UG038, 97USNG30, AD17, ADA, JR-FL, SF162 did not have off-the-shelf references to enable sample-specific mapping. See Supplemental Table 1 for read counts by sample.

What was demonstrated for HIV in its DNA form (Gener 2019) also applies for HIV in its RNA form: variation happens. Sequencing the viral strains and cloned constructs used for experiments in each laboratory remains important, because what is reported in a reference database for a given virus may not necessarily be the same as the viruses propagated in a laboratory. We recommend using sample-specific references for mapping when possible together with sequence-verifying constructs used to make viruses in each lab to catch any lurking putative SNVs (Gener 2019).

docs.title: Reference HIV-1 viruses are variable.
docs.text: Up until 2020, HIV was the most studied human pathogen, and yet we found 167-35 redundant = 132 non-redundant pSNVs across 9 HIV-1 reference strains. Some occurred in previously camouflaged repetitive LTRs, but most occurred in gene bodies, some contributing to alterations in protein-coding potential. In this work we leveraged sequencing multiple related strains with mapping to their predecessors to simulate true positive variants, which supported our use of single references to evaluate SNVs. Long read native RNA sequencing on the ONT MinION with R9.4.1 RevD flow cells was robust and sufficient to detect real sequence variability at the single-molecule level, except for at areas in and around homopolymers. While not a complete solution yet, long read native RNA sequencing offers the ability to tie SNVs together, to define segments of HIV haplotypes directly, and to move away from the concept of quasispecies (Lauring and Andino 2010; Pandit and Boer 2014) toward defining real viral haplotypes. An extension of this capability is the ability to perform comparative transcriptomics almost immediately after sample acquisition (Figure 5), including determining drug resistance profiles based on existing public databases (Rhee et al. 2003; Shafer 2006) (Supplemental Figure 11).

docs.title: Homopolymers
docs.text: As previously reported (Gener 2019; Loman, Quick, and Simpson 2015) for DNA ONT, per-read variability in native RNA ONT data was higher near homopolymers (runs of the same base) (Supplemental Figure 3). ONT is also known for lower per-base accuracy compared to short-read next generation sequencing platforms. These may be overcome by evaluating neighbor SNVs (Supplemental Figure 4). New developments include improved basecalling models and a new double-header R10.3 nanopore, which has been showing improved handling of homopolymers, with slight drop in per-read accuracy. When comparing sequences, the errors at homopolymers are observed consistently across reads, and become negligible when comparing similarly processed samples. For the first time, we were able to compare individual reads from mostly incomplete virion genomes with simple cladistics and saw that reads successfully grouped based on sample identity (Figure 5).

docs.title: Suitability of ONT for HIV sequencing
docs.text: Comparing classic RNA-seq to native RNA-seq, each technology has its pros and cons. Classic RNA-seq, usually cDNA synthesis optionally followed by PCR, can be sensitive, specific, and cheaper with newer high-throughput sequencers (example: Illumina, BGI) and higher fidelity PCR. While PCR enhances sensitivity (to this day, it is important for detecting viral sequences at low copy numbers (Worobey et al. 2016; Yamaguchi et al. 9000)), a downside is that information can be lost if PCR is used during library prep (Supplemental Figure 12). Direct (PCR-free) cDNA, or using long-read DNA sequencing (PacBio (Karen E. Ocwieja et al. 2012), ONT (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020)), can also recuperate sequence information from samples with relatively higher throughput than native RNA-seq currently. It will be important to address sequencing throughput and sequence biases when developing this nascent technology. At present, it is possible to sequence and compare viral isolates as contigs and for the first time as individual virus genomes as individual reads (Figure 5), as well as to determine drug resistance profiles from contigs (Supplemental Figure 11) or individual reads. A benefit that is unique to native RNA sequencing on ONT devices is the ability to detect base modifications as well. Work is ongoing to evaluate the raw signal from these experiments, and to evaluate new ONT RNA tools for use with HIV.

docs.title: Closing the distance on HIV-1 with longer reads
docs.text: Current limitations of the approaches used in the present work to study HIV-1 RNA are similar to those reported for HIV-1 DNA (Gener 2019), and include: 1) the cost of long-read sequencing, compared to the cheaper short-read DNA-seq (classic RNA-seq); 2) long RNA extraction methods in diseased tissue; and 3) lower per-base accuracy (mid 90’s vs. 98-99%), including difficulty near small repeats such as homopolymers (Supplemental Figure 3). Furthermore, a unique major limitation to native RNA sequencing is 4): 3’ bias. For all nucleic acid sequencing: full coverage does not necessarily mean even coverage. As the price of long-read sequencing continues to decrease, and as the technology improves, the cost of obtaining usable data from native RNA long-read sequencing will become negligible compared to the ability to answer new questions. Classic RNA-seq had a problem with 3’ bias, but the issue was eventually overcome (Sheng et al. 2017). Future work will advance toward higher coverage complete observations of HIV viral mRNAs, including virion genomes in in vivo HIV models and from patient samples. Long-read sequencing is an important emerging tool defining the post-scaffold transcriptomic era, allowing for the characterization of these previously obscured functional units at the intersection between host and pathogen transcriptomes.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Advancing HIV informatics in the RNA space: On “transductions”
Chapter abstract
docs.text: In Chapter 8 we use LTR phasing from Chapter 5 to complete careful analysis of Nguyen et al.’s datasets, as well as our own native/direct RNA virion sequences. Our findings support precursor spliced mRNA products derived from producer cells are predominant virion cargo. Few RT products were generated between 12-24 hours after infection of CD4+ T cells with pseudotyped HIV-1 NL4-3 or after transfection with pNL4-3 in HeLa. These findings support a shift away from the notion that HIV virion mRNA is predominantly unspliced and suggests packaged HIV splice isoforms play a dominant role in acute infections.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Objective: Plasmid pNL4-3 is a synthetic HIV-1 proviral construct which we recently confirmed has distinct long terminal repeats (LTRs). NL4-3 LTRs are expected to homogenize upon infection, whereby the 5’ NY5 LTR copies itself during reverse transcription within hours of infecting a new cell. However, this has not been demonstrated directly. We compared NL4-3 LTRs during acute in vitro infection to follow LTR homogenization.

Design: We completed retrospective analysis of long-read cDNA data from HIV1-NL43-infected CD4+ T cells GEO:GSE138425 (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020), and native/direct RNA sequencing (manuscript in prep).

Methods: Previously basecalled data was mapped to pNL4-3 reference (GenBank:AF324493.2) with minimap2 -splice in Galaxy and locally and visualized the results in the Integrative Genomics Viewer. We sorted reads per base at position AF324493.2:9,624; base 1).

Results: LTRs were phased incidentally using reads longer than ~654 bases (the length of the NL4-3 LTRs). A minority of reads mapping to the 3’ LTR exhibited the expected 98 base-long 5’ R. This ratio did not change over the time course evaluated. Native RNA had fewer homogenized reads before and after infection.

Conclusions: LTR phasing revealed that LTR homogenization did not happen often. A possible explanation is that primary transcripts from pNL4-3 were packaged, and that these represented most HIV-mapping reads at evaluated timepoints. Our observation demonstrates the utility of long-read sequencing to advance the study of HIV biology, and the need to question past assumptions about experimental models.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The study of HIV is tied to the production of HIV-1 virions. Investigators assume that virions from producer cell lines like 293T can sustain the full viral replication cycle. Part of that cycle involves transcription of full-length unspliced HIV-1, from the transcription start site of the 5’ LTR to a termination point in the 3’ LTR, followed by processing and packaging of these full-length unspliced HIV-1 genome equivalents into budding virions. Supernatant from transfected producer cell lines is collected and used for transduction (in vitro infection) of susceptible cells, such as primary CD4+ T cells enriched from fresh peripheral mononuclear cells.

Details of what happens during the production of HIV-1 virions have been obscured by the complex HIV replication cycle (https://viralzone.expasy.org/5096). HIV replication is often modeled following reverse transcription of single-stranded forward/positive/coding/sense virion-packaged mRNA to generate presumably identical double-stranded cDNA intermediates (Figure 1B: HIV-1 virion is modeled as a virus particle with 2 full-length genome equivalents). This cDNA complex with viral and host proteins forms a preintegration complex. This complex is transported to the infected cell’s nucleus across the host cell microtubule network. Viral integrase catalyzes cDNA end processing and strand transfer, successfully ending with integration of HIV cDNA and establishment of HIV provirus.

Figure 1B: HIV-1 virion is modeled as a virus particle with 2 full-length genome equivalents.

Red is pNL4-3 sequence. Blue sequence simplifies expected change. Compare to Figure 4. For simplicity, circularized cDNA is not displayed.

Until recently, sequencing technology had been unable to provide longer direct observations of HIV-1 nucleic acid intermediates, obscuring events of reverse transcription (Hu and Hughes 2012). We recently demonstrated Oxford Nanopore’s long-read sequencing’s ability to distinguish variants between HIV-1’s long terminal repeats (LTRs), also called LTR phasing (Alejandro R Gener et al. 2021). While virion mRNA does not include full-length LTRs, virion mRNA does encode segments of LTR: U3, R repeats, and U5. The most common lab strain of HIV-1 is NL4-3 (Figure 1A: Long terminal repeats are proviral features). This is a synthetic chimera between NY5 on the 5’ side and LAV/HXB2 on the 3’ side (hence “NL…”). NL4-3 as a provirus template may be modeled as: (U3A-RA-U5A)NY5-HIV-(U3B-RB-U5B)LAV/HXB2. As HIV-1 mRNA, LTRs are split as 5’R-U5-HIV-U3-3’R. In our earlier work we confirmed that NL4-3 had distinct 5’ U3 and 3’ U3, as well as 5’ R and 3’ R segments (Figure 3: pNL4-3 imbues pNL4-3 transcripts with distinct R repeats). Nguyen et al. recently published in vitro experiments on CD4+ T and HeLa cells infected with pseudotyped NL4-3 viral supernatants. We expected to be able to observe LTR homogenization in other’s cDNA Oxford Nanopore long-read (ONT) datasets, as well as in our native/direct ONT. This would mean 100% of LTRs would become (U3B-RA-U5A) (Figure 2: HIV-1 reverse transcription and LTR homogenization (copying)).

Figure 1A: Long terminal repeats are proviral features.

Figure adapted from Gener et al. 2021. BioRxiv. pNL4-3 is a plasmid encoding NL4-3 sequence. This plasmid is used to generate pseudotyped NL4-3. pNL4-3 is an important molecular biology tool used widely. A search in Addgene (addgene.org) on 7/13/21 for “lenti” returned 11,443 plasmid hits, many of which contained modified NL4-3 sequence.

Figure 3: pNL4-3 imbues pNL4-3 transcripts with distinct R repeats.

Plasmid pNL4-3 (GenBank:AF324493.1) was used to make pseudotyped NL4-3 (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020). gRNA contained in such pseudotyped viruses is expected to be primary mRNA derived from host transcription from the plasmid template. These virions are then used for subsequent transductions. Reverse-transcribed NL4-3 cDNA sequence should have homogenized 5’ and 3’ LTRs, such that each 3’ LTR converts into the 5’ sequence. Figure method: Above sequences were input into MAFFT online server (https://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/software/), which implemented the following commands: mafft --reorder --auto input. L-INS-i method was automatically selected (Katoh et al. 2005). The 5’ and 3’ U5 regions of pNL4-3 are identical and so cannot be used for LTR phasing.

Figure 2: HIV-1 reverse transcription and LTR homogenization (copying).

R repeats are expected to homogenize along with LTRs. R repeats are features of both HIV mRNA and DNA. Full-length LTRs are only features of HIV DNA. Blue/red coloring in this figure is arbitrary and is meant to distinguish between RNA template and cDNA. Adapted from (SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics n.d.).

docs.title: Datasets, reference, and bioinformatics
docs.text:
Data from (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020) were reanalyzed as follows. Long-read cDNA ONT datasets from HeLa and primary CD4+ T cells (GEO:GSE138425; BioProject:PRJNA511009) were mapped to pNL4-3 reference (GenBank:AF324493.2) with Minimap2 (Li 2018) -splice in Galaxy (usegalaxy.org) (Afgan et al. 2016) or locally. Alignments (sorted .bam and .bai files) were visualized individually in the Integrative Genomics Viewer (Robinson et al. 2011). Aligned reads were grouped in IGV at base AF324493.1:9,624, corresponding to the R variant 97delT (97 based on first base in G triplet defining HIV TSS (Alejandro R. Gener et al. 2021; Gener 2021) and thus beginning of each R). Per (Nguyen Quang et al. 2020), “INF” coded for infection/transduction. “TF” coded for transfection. Cells were either transduced with VSVg-pseudotyped NL4-3 virus-containing supernatant, or transfected with pNL4-3, and subsequently lysed after 12-24 hours post infection (hpi) or hours post transfection. The authors reported that their virus preps included a DNAse step prior to transduction. For their time course experiment, the authors used SMART-Seq v4 Ultra Low Input RNA kit (Clontech) for cDNA synthesis. Sequencing data was collected with MinKNOW software (v 3.3.2), and basecalling was performed with Guppy (v 3.1.5). Their non-time course data was made with SQK-LSK108 and EXP-PBC001 kits, sequencing data was collected with MinKnow (v 1.10.23 and 1.11.5), and basecalling was performed with Albacore (v 2.1.10 and 2.2.7).

Data from our native/direct RNA sequencing is discussed elseware (Alejandro R. Gener et al. 2021; Gener 2021; Gener and Kimata 2019).

docs.title: LTRs do not homogenize between 12-24 hours post infection (hpi)
docs.text:
Lack of homogenization was independent of whether the sample pertained to a transduction or transfection, and independent of cell line (CD4+ T cell vs. HeLa). Table 1: CD4+ T cell allele count at AF324493.2:9,624; Table 2: HeLa cell allele count at AF324493.2:9,624. Reads were generally sufficiently long to obviate read filtering (Figure 4: Example HIV-1 NL4-3 cDNA from CD4+ T cells 12 hours post-infection). No single nucleotide variants (SNVs) were immediately apparent when viewing mapped. The ends of the R repeats do not contain homopolymers, dimer or trimer repeats which are known to be problematic for unpolished and/or unassembled ONT sequences, here called reads. While many 3’ reads were truncated upstream of AF324493.2:9,624/R 97delT, there were hundreds of reads available to be able to accumulate a robust number of observations. Reads were truncated past the canonical polyA site, suggesting the sequences did not derive directly from contaminating plasmid. Splice patterns were commonly seen. However, coverage depth was not sufficient to appreciate many full-length spliced isoforms which were also homogenized. Homogenized signal was most likely derived from transcription off nascent HIV-1 NL4-3 cDNA or new proviral integrants in infected cells. The former is more likely, given that relative amount of homogenized R did not change across 12-24 hpi.

Figure 4: Example HIV-1 NL4-3 cDNA from CD4+ T cells 12 hours post-infection.

This IGV snapshot is from CD4+ T cells infected at 12 (top) and 24 (bottom) hours post infection.

Our native virion sequencing experiments included 3 virions based on NL4-3: NLAD8, which had very high coverage, NL4-3 which had low to moderate coverage, both derived from only pNL4-3 (as opposed to pseudotyped pNL4-3 NL4-3). A third virion dataset, HIV-SX, was believed to be made in a similar way as our NL4-3 and NLAD8, however exact details were not available (Table 3: Virion allele count at AF324493.2:9,624 from native/direct RNA; Figure 5: Native RNA (my datasets from Chapter 7)). None of these virion preps exhibited effectively any LTR homogenization. This is consistent with virions made from primary transcripts and prior to RT in the infected cells.

Figure 5: Native RNA (my datasets from Chapter 7).

Example native RNA (NLAD8 dataset from Chapter 7)

Native RNA sequencing (also called direct RNA sequencing) captures sequence information from mRNA directly without the need for cDNA sequencing. NLAD8 virion (top) was produced by transfecting 293T cells with a pNLAD8 AIDS Reagent Program number ARP-11346 (method (Gener et al. n.d.)). NLAD8 is a strain of virus with NL4-3 backbone and env from AD8 (GenBank:AF004394.1). Supernatant was collected 48 hours post infection. HIV-SX/SX (bottom) virion was produced by infecting/transducing cultured peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with HIV-SX, which is a strain of virus with NL4-3 backbone and env from JR-FL. Supernatant was collected over 10-15 days post infection. These virion preps are from supernatant of transfected producer cells (NLAD8) before infection, or infected peripheral blood mononuclear cells (HIV-SX/SX) after infection, so we expect minimal to no RT products in fresh virion lysates (as opposed to acutely infected cell lysates), and therefore no R homogenization. LTR homogenization was expected in cell lysates during acute infection. Spliced HIV in virions and predominant mRNA in infected cell lysates was not expected long after infection.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text: Reverse transcription is believed to occur within 8-12 hours post-infection of host cell (Iordanskiy et al. 2006). cDNA from RT is detectable within 4 hours post infection (hpi) (Hu and Hughes 2012). So, it was reasonable to detect homogenized sequence within 12-24 hpi.

docs.title: R repeat coordinate change
docs.text: The HIV-1 NL4-3 R repeats are occasionally noted to start at the second G in the G triplet. However, high-quality long-read cDNA sequencing by Nguyen et al. 2020 and our preliminary work Gener et al. 2021 (bioRxiv) verifying NL4-3 LTR sequence support reassignment of the R repeat as including the full G triplet. Nguyen et al.’s datasets were generated with PCR barcoded ONT. The ONT PCR adapter would add an A tail, resulting in either an A or a T on the sequenced strand. This would increase the lengths of the 5’ HIV-1 M B NY5 R to 98 from 97, and the 3’ HIV-1 M B LAV to 99 to

docs.title: Pseudotyped lentiviral preps support Hybrid Segmented Retrovirus model
docs.text:
Nguyen et al. extracted total mRNA from was infected CD4+ T cells and recovered mostly spliced HIV-mapping reads. These reads were almost identical to mapped segments of in silico pNL4-3 reference genome sequence. The relative lack of error in Nguyen et al.’s cDNA datasets speaks to the accuracy of the host 293T producer cell transcriptional machinery. Although we did see that some RT products are spliced, most sequences were likely not reverse transcribed in the CD4+ T cells. This matches work by another French group reporting spliced products participating in RT. Together, this supports an idea of HIV virion packaging splice isoforms. Future work may include virion prepared from producer cells lines with stably integrated HIV-1 as opposed to pseudotyped plasmid-derived lentiviral preps.

R repeats withing LTRs are normally identical in natural infections after RT. NL4-3’s distinct Rs make it a valuable tool to be able to follow LTR homogenization. In the future, there will be a need for more long-read data from cell lines latently infected with NL4-3 HIV. Otherwise LTR homogenization dynamics may remain unknown as one will not be able to see differences between LTRs.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
HIV researchers and others using lentiviral vectors assume that the lentiviruses they make during virus prep are in fact “HIV virion.” A rampant assumption about these virions is that they package two copies of full-length unspliced virus genomes or engineered templates. The results of our reanalyses of others’ high-quality HIV-1 NL4-3 cDNA datasets challenge these assumptions. We found that the majority of traceable ONT cDNA reads were in fact pNL4-3 transcripts likely made in producer cells (Figure 6: HIV-1 virions exist along a spectrum, and most mRNA in acute infection system comes from producer cell BEFORE infection). These were in fact mostly spliced forms of pNL4-3 mRNAs. Additionally, our results support the view that HIV-1 virions may regularly package HIV-1 splice isoforms. This is consistent with our observations of splice isoforms in virion-associated mRNA (Alejandro R. Gener et al. 2021; Gener 2021; Gener and Kimata 2020). Taken together, it seems best to recalibrate our understanding of pseudotyped lentiviral vectors as more like transfections from the primary plasmid sequence used rather than prior assumed transductions with full-length viral genome equivalents or templates.

Figure 6: HIV-1 virions exist along a spectrum, and most mRNA in acute infection system comes from producer cell BEFORE infection.

HIV-1 virions exist along a spectrum.

Red is pNL4-3 sequence. Blue sequence simplifies expected change. Compare to Figure 1B. Details of virion mRNA are discussed separately (Gener, AR. 2021. HIV Informatics. Chapter 7.; manuscript in prep). For simplicity, circularized cDNA is not displayed.

Future work should determine whether LTRs homogenize at a higher efficiency when virus is prepared from cell lines with sequence-verified and stably integrated NL4-3. As a part of sequence verification, it will be important to determine HIV copy number integration site location, and to define the internal structure of each integration site in those systems. This work has broad implications for retroviral research, as well as for use of lentiviral vectors. Long-read sequencing has become an important tool providing new insights into decades-old experimental procedures.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Maximizing HIV sequence information from heterogeneous samples
Chapter Abstract
docs.text:
In the previous chapters, I summarized our historical progress revisiting HIV through the HIV Informatics framework. We began our journey by sequence-verifying pHXB2_D, a key historical reagent, salvaging this resource from the dustbin of history. We didn’t just sequence-verify it. We compared new long-read nanopore DNA sequencing with the closest thing to a gold standard for HIV plasmid verification, single-end sequencing. The Center for Computational & Integrative Biology DNA Core at Massachusetts General Hospital we used in Chapter 5 used single-end 150 bp sequencing, and this was the “best” verification reported in the AIDS Reagent Program. Our approach enabled unambiguous long terminal repeat (LTR) phasing, which clarified the HXB2 record. It also enabled LTR phasing in a control NL4-3-based plasmid. This incidental finding has broad implications. pNL4-3 has distinct LTRs, specifically R repeats. Using long-read sequencing on high-quality NL4-3 long-read data from Nguyen et al. 2020, it was possible to phase LTRs. Remarkably, our reanalyses revealed that most of the mRNA in CD4+ T cells transduced with VSV-pseudotyped HIV-1 NL4-3 between 12-24 hours post-infection (hpi) derived from primary pNL4-3 transcripts from the producer 293T cell lines. Only about 20% of transcripts were reverse-transcribed, evinced by having completed LTR homogenization or copying of the 5’ R to the 3’ side. This raises interesting points to consider when designing all future lentiviral transduction experiments. Antiviral sensing pathways might be artifactually stimulated by such transfections, instead of transductions. Our reanalyses also draw into question the very nature of transductions with lentiviral vectors. Did these ever behave like we thought they did?

By sequencing HIV virion mRNA without PCR, we were able to recapitulate splicing patterns seen historically and in new high-quality long-read datasets. Our experiments also deviated from other’s cDNA datasets in several important ways. First, our transcription start sites (TSS) differed from other’s cDNA experiments. This was an artifact of native RNA sequencing and was important to demonstrate for HIV samples. We now have an excellent understanding of how the HIV genome might appear in control DNA and RNA samples, serving as a fortified foundation for assessing HIV information in more complex samples. In this chapter, we will explore HIV sequence variability from natural human infections. Post-mortem brain specimens from patients with HIV encephalopathy (HIVE) from the Manhattan Brain Bank were evaluated.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
HIV is well-known to infect brain tissues after HIV infection. While the brain has been recognized as a discreet compartmentalization (Korber et al. 1994), the exact cell(s) making up the HIV reservoir(s) in the brain remain undefined. It remains unknown whether infected brain cells can serve as reservoir, sustaining full viral replication cycle.

HIV reservoirs are populations of cells capable of sustaining the full HIV replication cycle. Two classic examples are CD4+ T cells and macrophages. In a generic HIV reservoir population, one would expect to see 3 things with RNA-seq: HIV mapping reads, signatures of HIV splicing, and distinct sequence variability as evidence of compartmentalization (e.g., SNVs, small in-frame SVs) between patients and between sampled sites (if reservoir) within the same patient.

Evidence of HIV replication may take the form of HIV mRNA in the case of gene expression as a function of mRNA abundance. In addition to HIV coverage as read depth, signatures of spliced HIV reads may be construed as indirect evidence of full replication, and HIV virion is historically modeled as unspliced HIV. Therefore, splice HIV must then come from activated integrated provirus or active unintegrated HIV cDNA.

Retroviruses like HIV-1 have high mutation rates (1/10,000 to 1/100,000) (Menéndez-Arias 2009). If HIV replication were happening, we would expect to see HIV variability cluster by cell type. For example, new acquired variants might occur in neurons if HIV made it inside that hypothetical reservoir and continued to replicate within that population of cells. Sequence divergence in a compartment would be evidence for virus evolution, supporting a given tissue’s reservoir status.

Based on other’s observations, we hypothesized that Mφ/MG cells would express the highest amount of HIV relative to the other cell types assayed. We hypothesized that astrocytes would have lower levels of HIV gene expression, suggesting incomplete or inefficient HIV replication. We hypothesized that neurons, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs would have low or no HIV gene expression. We hypothesized that mapping to pan-HIV reference may increase recovery of HIV sequences compared to mapping to HXB2 (GenBank:K03455.1) or HXB2-like (GenBank:AF033819.3) HIV-1 reference genomes. We hypothesized that mapping to bespoke (sample-specific) assemblies will be higher than mapping to HXB2 (GenBank:K03455.1) or HXB2-like (GenBank:AF033819.3) HIV-1 reference genomes.

docs.title: Brain biopsy source
docs.text: Cadaveric brain biopsy from patients who died from HIV encephalopathy were obtained by Dr. Susan Morgello at the Manhattan Brain Bank under appropriate institutional supervision.

docs.title: Tissue processing
docs.text:
Flow sorting was used to enrich for pools of macrophages/microglia (Mφ) expressing Irf8, neurons expressing NeuN, oligodendrocytes expressing Oligo2, and triple-negative cells were considered astrocytes mixed with small amounts of other cell types. Ensemble (pooled) RNA-seq was performed on these pools.

Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) was adapted for single nuclear isolation and sequencing. gene expression signatures were used to cluster reads into microglia (MG or Mφ), Myeloid cells (monocytes/macrophages), neurons (Neu), oligodendrocytes (Olig), oligodendrocytes precursor cells (OPC), and astrocytes (Ast).

docs.title: Bespoke (sample-specific) assemblies
docs.text:
Human (hg38) reads mapped with STAR (Dobin et al. 2013) were excluded from downstream HIV assemblies and mapping. Filtered non-human reads were assembled into scaffolds with metaSPAdes (Bankevich et al. 2012) in Galaxy (Afgan et al. 2016). Scaffolds were mapped to the HXB2-like HIV-1 reference sequence AF033819.3 with minimap2 20% (Li 2018) in Galaxy and/or locally. Minimap2 --splice was also evaluated with negligible performance increases. Forward-oriented scaffolds were pasted sequentially into new SnapGene files [source]. Any reverse-oriented scaffolds relative to AF033819.3 (like NC_001802.1) were pasted into temporary SnapGene files and “flipped” to assume forward orientation, and then brought into the working manual assembly. Gaps were filled as bridges with sequences from AF033819.3. Clipped areas from mapping were cut from SnapGene segments. Round 1 manual assemblies were checked by aligning relevant scaffold “nodes” to evaluate for appropriate manual clipping. Features were imported from AF033819.3 with fuzzy mapping (e.g., “Find similar DNA sequences” and “allow a mismatch or gap/insertion every 10-4 bases”), and adjusted based on open reading frames (ORFs) identified by SnapGene. At this point, ORFs approximated most imported features. Sequences were saved as .dna (SnapGene proprietary format) and .fasta as v1.n assemblies, where n is the number of haplotypes resulting from distinct scaffolds.

For visualization of bespoke assemblies in the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) (Robinson et al. 2011), .fasta files and .gff3 files were used. At the time of this work, feature export as .gff3 was not supported by SnapGene. To make gff3, .dna with annotations were saved as “GenBank – Standard” formatted files. These were converted in Galaxy with “GenBank to GFF3 converter (Galaxy Version 1.1).” The output file’s first/leftmost column contained the phrase “Expected”. This was replaced with the chromosome number (text after “>” in fasta header, ending in space), to be able to visualize annotations in IGV.

Data was mapped to new v1.n assemblies to evaluate coverage improvement, and to modify bridges where sample sequences diverged from AF033819.3. HISAT2 (Kim, Langmead, and Salzberg 2015) was used to map HIV-1 reads to bespoke assemblies.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: We tested several approaches to retrieve HIV information from samples. In order of relative total yield, we tried 1.) mapping reads to HXB2 (GenBank:K03455.1 which is a single linear reference as a single FASTA file), then 2.) mapping reads to a pan-HIV genome concatenated multi-FASTA, and lastly 3.) assembling HIV genomes de novo from Mφ/MG cells, and then re-mapping input reads onto the new bespoke references to assess minor allele frequencies which were not incorporated into each bespoke reference. The later returned the highest yields, including increasing detection of spliced reads. Default SPAdes failed to produce assemblies. We think this is because natural HIV reads are very noise. The tuning of SPAdes in metaSPAdes was able to handle the natural HIV sequence heterogeneity.

docs.title: Mapping
docs.text:
We assessed HIV-1 coverage by mapping (HISAT2 (Kim et al. 2015) or Minimap2 (Li 2018)) non-human (hg38) cell-sorted ensemble RNA-seq reads to HIV-1 HXB2 K03455.1. Ensemble RNA-seq samples were heterogeneous, with high background. As such, HIV-1 genome assembly was deferred for these samples. We next assessed HIV-1 coverage by mapping non-human (hg38) single-nucleus RNA-seq reads to HIV-1 HXB2 K03455.1. Microglial cells had the highest HIV burden. Mapping to HIV pan-genome failed. Instead, reads would map to parts of sequences, leaving many split reads across references. We found that supplying one reference was better than many at once.

Assembly

Coverage against HIV-1 HXB2 K03455.1 was too low to assemble HIV-1. De novo genome assembly was attempted with all non-human (hg38) single-nucleus RNA-seq reads, per sample. MetaSPAdes (Bankevich et al. 2012) implemented in Galaxy (Afgan et al. 2016) was successful at assembling HIV-1 genomes in high coverage microglial samples. We were able to assemble three complete HIV-1 genomes from 3 different post-mortem HIV encephalopathy cases (Figure 2: HIV-1_mhbb629, a complete HIV-1 genome assembled from a patient who died of HIV encephalopathy (HIVE); Figure 3: HIV-1_010017, a complete HIV-1 genome assembled from a patient who died of HIV encephalopathy (HIVE); Figure 4: HIV-1_010070, a complete HIV-1 genome assembled from a patient who died of HIV encephalopathy (HIVE)).

Uses only short reads and coverage to predict models. These are not seen in higher-quality long-read datasets (Gener et al. 2021; Nguyen Quang et al. 2020; Ocwieja et al. 2012). Reference: bespoke from sample 10017. Dataset: scRNA-seq microglia (MG).

Figure 6: Variants detected AFTER maximizing HIV information supports limited viral evolution in non-microglial cells.

Variants were noted after maximizing HIV information by mapping reads to bespoke assemblies. Variants found in non-microglial cells but absent in microglial (MG) cells support independent evolution. However, absence of additional coverage and splice signals suggest that replication stops shortly after reverse transcription. Human-mapping data was filtered prior to analysis, and each integration occurs pseudorandomly, so incidental integration site analyses are not possible. Our model is like the Trojan horse proposed by others (e.g., Jay A. Levy) whereby infected microglia may produce high amounts of HIV, infecting neighboring cells. Neighboring cells may not be able to support HIV replication much beyond RT.

docs.title: Remapping
docs.text: Repeat mapping (remapping) against bespoke sample-specific assembly references increase mapping by 2-4x. Splice junctions we much more obvious when mapping to bespoke reference. Minor variants in microglial samples were retained, as evidenced by fewer read variability compared to when mapping against HXB2. Coverage in non-microglial cells was too low to assemble, and usually didn’t recuperate splice junctions. Despite low coverage in non-microglial cells, coverage sufficient to detect variants unique to each non-microglial compartment. This supports at least abortive infection of these cells during acute HIVE.

docs.title: Discussion and Conclusion
docs.text: Natural infections are distinct from in vitro infections in that natural patient/community-acquired HIV-1 sequences have long since diverged from HXB2-like sequences. We developed a strategy to efficiently make reference-quality and patient-specific bespoke HIV-1 genomes from cells expected to exhibit high HIV gene expression. Coverage was too low to attempt transcript modeling, however there was clearly evidence of splicing after reads were remapped to their bespoke assemblies. Future work may evaluate long-read approaches to recover isoform information from brain. Long-read approaches may be combined with
